#6741. Why Are These Huge Arc’teryx Boots Suddenly Going Viral?

​Where were you during the Great Arc’teryx Jacket Phenomenon of 2022? If you’ve forgotten, the cult Canadian outdoors label went viral when young men on TikTok began filming themselves in the shower to demonstrate the hypnotic water-repelling ability of their Gore-Tex jackets. The attention only seemed to further cement Arc’teryx’s techy outerwear as an inescapable part of the menswear landscape. Now, the Vancouver brand appears to have another crossover hit on its hands: a hulking beast of a winter boot.

The Postour is a two-in-one design that combines a weatherproof outer boot with a removable insulated slipper tucked inside. In what the brand calls “full-boot mode,” the high collar cinches shut with a utility cord, sealing you off from the elements. The idea is that you can spend the day stomping through snow and slush, then shed the outer shell and lounge around in the slippers. Though it almost looks like a chalk bag sprouted a foot, the silhouette still carries the sleek, hyperfunctional minimalism the brand is known and loved for. The oddness of the design seems to be part of the appeal.

Naturally, it’s equipped with all the technical bells and whistles you’d expect from Arc’teryx: a gnarly Vibram Arctic Grip outsole, weatherproof Gore-Tex shell, and the label’s proprietary Coreloft insulation. Perhaps most covetably, there’s also a giant skeletal bird logo—known to diehards as the “deadbird”—on the side. The same logo has helped make the brand’s beanies a favorite of everyone from Timothée Chalamet to Frank Ocean.

Much like Arc’teryx’s Gore-Tex jackets before it, the Postour has become unmissable on the men’s side of the fashion algorithm. It’s a viral object of desire for a certain type of menswear guy fluent in microtrends. (This is hardly the first time we’ve seen a polarizing boot take over the algorithm, after all.) The is-this-ugly-or-cool discourse only adds fuel to the fire—and the fact that the boots resemble a sought-after design from Yeezy Season 8 certainly doesn’t hurt. TikTok and Instagram are chock full with videos of dudes excitedly unboxing their boots, blasting them with hoses, and customizing them with colored wax. As a result of all this digital buzz, the $300 boot has been drifting in and out of stock on the official Arc’teryx website. At one point last week, it was fully sold out; as of press time, only a couple of sizes remain in stock (though REI currently has a full size run).

Of course, winter footwear has its own pantheon of heavy hitters, from L.L.Bean’s iconic Bean Boot to Sorel’s felt-lined stompers and Timberland’s “40 Below” Super Boot. Whether the Postour will earn a place alongside those classics remains to be seen. For now, Arc’teryx has made the rare winter boot that’s as hyped up online as it is useful in a snowstorm. Good luck getting your hands on a pair.

#6740. The 6 Best Hair Rollers for Supermodel Volume

Salon-level bounce, no appointment necessary.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

If you've ever been envious of a big, bouncy blowout à la a ’90s supermodel, I have amazing news: Those angelic waves are actually pretty simple to recreate—no salon visit required, promise! Even if you don't have the skills of a professional celebrity stylist (because I definitely don't), you can still achieve tons of volume with the right hair routine and the best hair rollers.

If you’re after va-va-volume, using your thermal round brush, multi-styler, or blow dryer on its own simply won’t cut it. A set of hair rollers is the key to long-lasting volume. As a long-haired beauty editor who loves nothing more than the way my hair looks after a salon blowout, I've tried pretty much every type of hair roller out there to DIY those same coveted waves at home. I also tapped expert hairstylists to share how to properly use these root-lifting tools, below.

Why we love it: These ceramic Velcro rollers are perfect for achieving that bouncy blowout look. They come in three different sizes so you can easily place them around the head, with the smallest being perfect for shorter layers and bangs. You won't have to worry about them falling out of your hair, either, since they're made with a self-grip surface and don't require any clips. Just roll ’em up, and you’re good to go.

Why we love it: Want to keep your hair effortlessly voluminous on the go? (Who doesn’t?!) Mane’s travel-friendly roller set will ensure your mane (heh) stays bouncy, no matter where you are in the world. The barrels on this six-piece set are self-gripping, too, so there’s no need to pack extra clips that are bound to get lost in the bottom of a bag.

Why we love it: If you've got a lot of hair, first, consider yourself blessed, but you might need more than the standard six-to-nine set of rollers. Luckily, this convenient kit comes with 36 (!!!) along with 18 metal clips to lock them in place. There are also long- and short-hair size options, so if you've got a bob, creating the perfect curls and waves will still be a breeze.

Beauty editor Beth Gillette loves the smallest size for her super-fine bixie lengths, “These are so gentle on my hair, even as I pull them out—I can see why the Pheloung sisters have such good hair,” she explains. “But I especially love the range of sizes and how many come in this chic case.”

Why we love it: If you want XXL volume without needing to re-wet your hair, a set of heated rollers is a one-and-done way to get the look of a defined blowout on already-dry hair. Not only do the T3 hot rollers have a dual temperature setting, but they have cool-grip edges, so you won't burn your precious fingers while setting them in place. The set even comes in a sleek case and has an auto-off setting—no need to question if you left them on while you're out at dinner (we’ve all been there).

Why we love it: While most rollers are made of plastic, these are constructed out of metal, which evenly distributes heat and really locks in the volume when you’re blowing out your hair at home. You might think that metal would slip right off your mane, but these have a self-grip exterior that latches onto your hair. (The set does come with clips if you need some extra support, though.) You shouldn’t be surprised if your hair still looks voluminous two or three days after using these.

Why we love it: Sure, you can sleep in hair rollers, but you probably won’t get a good night’s sleep. (I’m speaking from experience.) If you're looking for a comfortable method that will ensure tons of volume and gorgeous waves, look no further than Kitsch's Heatless Curling Set. It's made of soft satin, so there's no pulling or tugging, and it comes with two matching scrunchies to hold your hair perfectly in place overnight. When someone compliments your hair, you can literally say "I woke up like this."

Every hair roller is different, and each hair type will require unique steps. However, it's a good idea to keep these expert-recommended tips in mind if you're looking to achieve a bouncy blowout at home:

"The way your curlers and hair sets is the way that it is going to flow," explains Tippi Shorter, celebrity hairstylist and Mizani global artistic director. "Place the rollers at the crown of the head and roll your hair under the curler; that way, you will get more volume and body."

Joseph Maine, celebrity stylist and artistic director of Color Wow Hair, suggests using a brush and rollers that are on the larger side in order to achieve a smoother bouncy blowout. "The smaller they are, the more curls they're going to leave in your hair."

Use a diffuser attachment on a blow dryer to gently heat the rollers back up after each one has been placed. This will ensure that they are set perfectly. Then, keep the rollers in your hair for about 15 minutes or until they cool down completely.

In short: There’s no one-size-fits-all roller, and each type serves a slightly different purpose. You probably have seen quite a few throwback pics of supermodels getting glammed up with Velcro rollers, but times have changed, and rollers have evolved.

Hot and heatless rollers can be used to create the effortless and bouncy look you're going for—it just depends on the size of the roller and the process you use. And remember, the bigger the roller, the bouncier the hair. That means the smaller the roller, the tighter the curls will be.

Additionally, some rollers are made from ceramic or metal, while others are made of plastic. The ceramic and metal distribute heat better and are able to boost and lock in volume more easily. The plastic rollers are also effective, but their effects don’t last as long.

It depends on the type of roller you use and what your desired final look is. For example, if you’re hoping to create heatless curls, stick with satin or plastic rollers and sleep with them overnight for defined ringlets come morning. All rollers can boost volume, and if you want to restore bounce, they should be used on dry hair to lift your roots.

"Most people need to have extra moisture in the hair in order to get a hair roller style to stay," says Maine. To ensure that your hair is properly hydrated, apply blowout mousse, spray, or leave-in conditioner before styling.

#6739. Shop Our Favorite Celebrity Looks of the Week

Fall is finally here! If you’re wondering what to wear to embrace the drop in temperatures, we’re here to simplify matters with outfit ideas, courtesy of our favorite celebrities spotted on the streets. Consider this week’s edit your guide to everything from transitional fall looks to clever layering techniques, all infused with plenty of off-duty flair.

This week, celebrities embraced the seasonal chill, stepping out in their fall outerwear best. Jennifer Lawrence wore Auralee’s navy barn jacket for a walk in New York, styled with a graphic T-shirt, red pants, and a plaid button-down tied around her waist. Naomi Watts chose a double-breasted pinstripe blazer over a crisp white T-shirt and relaxed denim, finishing the look with playful accessories, including a floral brooch, an oversized-buckle belt, and a printed silk scarf. Both looks reinforced how a classic topper is truly the easiest way to pull together every fall outfit.

Meanwhile, guests at the CFDA Awards in New York offered a glimpse of what’s to come for occasion dressing as the holiday season approaches. Alexa Chung arrived in Tory Burch’s velvet robe dress and leather pumps in mustard tones, accessorizing with Elsa Peretti for Tiffany & Co. jewelry for a decadent finish. Hailey Bieber, too, embraced a gilded approach, leaning into the rich brocades and sumptuous embellishments seen on the spring 2027 runway. Her Saint Laurent skirt set, trimmed with faux-fur cuffs, was accented simply with strappy metallic heels for a touch of extra shine. Gold is having a moment, and there's no better time to embrace a little evening opulence for upcoming weddings, cocktail events, or festive celebrations.

Keep reading to discover these ideas and more, bringing timeless classics to life with a few standout finds, all reworked by the stars and completely shoppable.

Ahead, our favorite celeb outfits of the week.

Jennifer Lawrence was spotted wearing Auralee’s navy barn jacket for a walk in New York, styling it with her signature eclectic approach. #6737. With the Hunger Games Press Tour, Have We Reached the Final Frontier of Method Dressing?

The cast has offered a pointed take on the state of today’s red carpets

Another Hunger Games movie, a prequel to the initial series, premieres later this month, and with it comes another press tour full of fantastically far-fetched fashion. As the promotional events begin to stack up for Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, we are reminded of the familiar lore of this dystopian empire: In a fictionalized future America called Panem, the 12 districts that supply resources to the rich and powerful people of the Capitol are forced to send two children to fight to the death each year. The excess of the Capitol is signaled in the films via outlandish style, which the newest film’s cast members have been attempting to channel in their recent looks. The goal is to be extreme—but in an era of extremes on the red carpet, these over-the-top ensembles actually don’t look so out of place.

Elle Fanning plays a young Effie Trinket, who is essentially a Capitol stylist dressing the young “tributes” in all sorts of fanciful fashions—and doing the same for herself. (In the first film series, the character wore a lot of McQueen.) So far, Fanning’s press looks have deliberately channeled that outlandishness. For a London fan screening, she wore a gown from Robert Wun’s Fall 2026 couture collection that subverted ideas of childlike wonder. Her ensemble began in miniature with a music-box-style ballerina atop a bubblegum pink fascinator. The corresponding human-size gown features a doubled-up bodice, the outer layer appearing to peel off, above a full tulle skirt, all in that same dusty pink.

For her other appearances, Fanning has established a de facto uniform of precisely tailored skirt suits, each paired with some sort of coordinating fascinator tilted just so above her brow. She has selected a soft pink pleated skirt suit from Valentino complete with a ruffled collar, gloves, and a butterfly-trimmed chapeau; a sharp-shouldered version in a deep, almost reptilian satin green from Demna’s Gucci; and a floral, bow-embellished one from Vivienne Westwood. The looks are decidedly feminine in a manner that is at once both futuristic and retro in very Capitol fashion.

Fanning’s stylist Samantha McMillen has been vocal about the references to the character, with captions like “Gucci Effie | @demna puts “The Hunger” into @thehungergames,” and “Elle bringing 🦋 “Sunrise” 🦋 to the Academy Gala.” And it’s not just Fanning doing this either. Costar Mckenna Grace recently recreated a Katniss Everdeen Capitol tour look in which Katniss’s dress quite literally caught fire. Created by Vietnamese designer Cong Tri, who is known for his sculptural silhouettes, the recreation nixed the pyrotechnics but printed graphic flames onto the skirt and bodice. With the help of stylist Molly Dickson, Grace also revived Katniss’s wedding dress with a frothy white, silver-embellished gown by Monique Lhuillier.

I haven’t seen the most recent films, but all of them examine the same concept of this dystopian society propped up by the Hunger Games themselves at different points on a timeline. In the first film specifically, the older Trinket uses their version of a press tour to craft a narrative around Katniss and her fellow tribute Peeta Mellark and win favor among their audience through larger-than-life fashion. The aforementioned fire dress referenced Everdeen’s district’s coal mining industry, and the wedding dress was meant to create the illusion of a love story between the two of them. The series of looks is designed to be projected to the surrounding communities—and garner as much attention as possible. The characters can quite literally benefit later in the life-and-death-style games from the loyalties and sympathies the theatrics spawn.

It’s only in recent years that this idea of method dressing, or theming press tour looks around an actor’s current project, has become commonplace. It began in earnest with the work of Law Roach and Zendaya around the Dune and Spider-Man franchises, Challengers, and The Drama. It was perhaps commercially crystallized in 2023 by Andrew Mukamal and Margot Robbie with Barbie—a press tour that spawned so much digital attention it earned its own coffee-table book—and, more recently, Wuthering Heights. Now, it has proof of concept, attracting stars like Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande in their promotion of Wicked, the new cast of Sense and Sensibility, and Lili Reinhart’s rom-com references for The Love Hypothesis. At its most reductive, the tactic is a surefire way to drum up conversation on social media; at its best, a clever way to add depth to a project’s storytelling.

As press tours become more and more oriented towards social media, it’s difficult to isolate the influence of method dressing on the red carpet’s current proclivity towards extremes. Everyone is trying to capitalize on the sort of hype that the Met Gala ensembles can drum up. Your reference needs to be loud enough to cut through the noise—pyrotechnics optional. It’s perhaps why avant-garde, couture, and couture-level designers like Wun, who dressed a large handful of stars at this year’s Met Gala, are carving out more and more space among these sorts of promotional events. At the same time, brands like Standing Ground and Matieres Fecales—it’s only a matter of time before Fanning wears one of those skirt suits—are also gaining traction as stylists treat the red carpet more like a magazine editorial than an occasion to get dressed up.

Then last night, Grace added another layer. She and Dickson have begun to look outside the films to reference looks of Jennifer Lawrence’s own. Lawrence played Katniss in the first movies. For a Madrid premiere, she wore a Miss Sohee couture dress that paid homage to the Givenchy naked dress Lawrence wore for this year’s Golden Globes. It all feels very meta, calling into question the role of fashion in these promotional spaces, real or fictional. On the IRL Hunger Games red carpet, the reference is dystopian extravagance—but with the rise of method dressing and the corresponding celebration of larger, louder looks, has dystopian extravagance already become the norm? In this case, it may not be life and death, but it could make or break your movie.

#6736. Is 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York' Immediately the Best Watch Movie Ever?

There are plenty of great movie watches: James Bond’s OG Rolex Submariner, Hans Gruber’s Cartier Tank, or even Hamilton’s made-for-Interstellar Murph. But there are very few great watch movies that dig into the myriad layers of meaning that compel real-world collectors. In that way, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, which rolled out to theaters nationwide on October 30, is a timepiece-lover’s dream movie.

In the film, John Turturro gives an Oscar-buzzy performance as Harry Lehman, an aging New York hustler who has scraped by for decades without evolving with the world around him. He doesn’t have a phone, dances to vinyl records, pays at diners with cash, and rents Barbara Stanwych movies (“tapes,” he calls them) from the public library for his wife.

Naturally, Harry is drawn toward watches, both for his personal use as items to steal. Along the way of The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, there’s a cornucopia of watches and Easter eggs for collectors to appreciate: Director Noah Segan meticulously selected a watch to fit every character’s personality. It matters deeply to Segan whether a character is wearing a vintage Rolex Explorer 1016 or a modern Hublot; and the movie even gets deep into the inner workings of timepieces. A pawn shop owner, played by Steve Buscemi, deems a Patek Philippe “fugazi” and shows Harry the lack of jewels in the movement. Watches, as totems of an analog world imbued with personal and cultural history, aren’t just a detail, but a vital motif.

It’s clear that The Only Living Pickpocket in New York could only come from a writer-director embedded in the hobby themselves. And, in the future, Segan, along with the dealer Adam Golden who sourced the pieces for the film, plans to bring these essential watches to auction for charity. GQ talked with Segan about how he chose the film’s array of timepieces, the state of his own collection, and why he would make a terrible watch salesman.

Noah Segan: That’s a great question. I wouldn’t presume to jump on anybody else’s intent in terms of watches. I think obviously there are a lot of watches in movies that have become iconic. The first kind-of-nice watch I ever got myself was a TAG Heuer Monaco because I was such a huge fan of Steve McQueen and Le Mans. There are obviously a lot of watches that are worn. I don’t know how often they get woven into a story, but in our case, our story is not just about time, but time changing, time running out, and that in combination with very physical things, tactile things. We’ve got a pickpocket, he’s tactile. He touches you. The idea of a totem and an object representing those things started feeling very important to me, and watches do that for me.

I would probably be a very bad watch salesman simply because I would want to keep all my favorites. So I think maybe collector is where I should stay, but I’ve always been a very, for lack of a better term, sort of analog guy. I still shoot film with a camera. I spin records. I live in an old house. The classic car in the movie is my old car.

I was lucky enough to grow up in an environment that appreciates the marriage of engineering and art and history. To me, that Venn diagram is a solid circle when it comes to wristwatches. These are objects that can be beautiful, they can be sophisticated, they can represent personal historic endeavors and also the macrocosm of historic feats.

The idea of what a watch means when you think of it in terms of The Dirty Dozen [a WWII-era field watch for soldiers commissioned by Britain from 12 iconic Swiss watchmakers] being there for the military or [Paul] Newman’s Rolex Daytona and its engraving on the back that says, “Drive Carefully Me.” All of a sudden you’re talking about something bigger than us, a celebrity, probably one of the biggest celebrities of all time who did something absolutely crazy, which was not being a movie star, but being a race car driver. And yet his wife still said, “Drive Carefully Me.” So there’s the personal, there’s the promotional, there’s the macro and the micro, and they all are fascinating to me.

Well, a close friend of mine is Adam Golden, who has a company called Menta, is actually a watch dealer who deals in very specific, unique vintage watches of great provenance.

In considering the watch for Harry, I really wanted something that could bridge the gap between a very useful tool and something of value. And that watch represents a lot for people in that respect. There was a time when Harry was a younger man, and that would have been a really good, valuable, useful tool for him to have. It’s an understated watch. It’s easy to read. It can last through whatever you throw at it on the streets in New York.

And yet today it’s something of incredible value financially and also incredible value to him because it is his watch. It has been a tool for him. And I couldn’t think of a better example than that Rolex 1016 to represent that combination of factors. And so Adam found us that watch and loaned it to us to wear.

We built the other watches in the movie around [the 1016]. Giancarlo Esposito plays Detective Warren, [Harry’s] foil and mirror image. He both helps Harry and is keeping an eye on him. He wears a Tudor Tuxedo, which shares a lot of, as we say in the watch game, DNA with something like a Rolex Explorer. In fact, it was made by the same company, and yet it’s just a little different.

Steve [Buscemi’s character] wears a thin, gold Rolex Cellini on a gold bracelet that, again, is something that would have been definitely a luxury item back in the day and is an even bigger luxury item today, but still represents something of an older time. Meanwhile, the watch Dylan [a young mobster played by Will Price] has, the Hublot, is considered today to be a very flashy, modern watch. It has a modern chronograph movement. It’s made with very present-day materials. And in fact, he’s not wearing it. It’s stuffed into his gym bag, and he says, “I only wear that when I go out to flex,” because it doesn’t represent a daily tool to him.

All of these things were designed and lent to us by Adam Golden to talk about who these characters were and to reflect something about the characters in a world where the physical items and the physical representation matter.

I can walk you through all of it! We also had some interesting newer watches. We worked with an incredible team at Oris, a brand that’s been around forever, but remains really relevant. Victoria Morolis, who plays Eve, wears Oris. She’s a sort of younger hero in the movie and a punk computer hacker. She’s wearing the Oris Roberto Clemente, which is a watch that is very old-school in a lot of ways, but made with very 2026 technology.

She was wearing her very own gold Cartier tank. She said, “I am going to do this.” And we all said, “Of course you are, because you are the boss.”

Well, I have a personal feeling about that because I have a lot of knowledge of this stuff. This is my hobby, right? So to me, when I look at a 1016, I see history, I see Tenzing Norgay summiting Everest, whether that’s the actual truth or not. I am applying that to my perspective. And I’m also thinking about elegance in terms of what I like to wear. I’m thinking about how it sits on my wrist. I’m thinking about the simplicity in the design. And I can also see how someone else would appreciate the exact same thing about the Hublot: the work that went into skeletonizing that dial, the complication of a chronograph movement, and the mixture of metals and materials to make it. So I see both sides of it. I think because it is something so personal, it goes on your body. I think what ends up mattering is how you interpret that and whether you believe that one is of more value to you than the other stylistically.

Well, I think it sort of speaks to Harry’s world quite a bit. Harry comes from a world where if someone looked like they had money, they probably had money, right? And if they had nice shoes, they probably had a nice watch. And if they had a nice watch, they probably had money in their pocket. And you could do that math, and maybe it wouldn’t always be right, but these were educated guesses. And now we live in a world where a gold watch is not necessarily a gold watch. A Patek Philippe, presumably one of the most recognizable objects of value, is not necessarily an object of value. And to put that on Harry, to put that on a guy whose job it is to steal watches is, among other things, really a statement about him. And I guess in a wider sense that the world is not always what we think it is.

I think for the businessman at the beginning, he obviously has lots of nice suits and lots of nice shoes and he lives in a tall building on the Upper East Side and he’s got a camel hair coat and works in a fancy office. There are all these reasons to think that this guy is fancy and makes money. He doesn’t carry cash. You know what I mean? He wears Aldens, as we know, a fancy shoe, but he wears a fake watch. I think it speaks to where the world is right now, which is that it isn’t about honesty or dishonesty. There are shades of gray, and we exist in a bit of a gray world.

Great question. I think he knows that it’s fake. I think there is a world now where people—and I don’t think it’s just for watches, I think it’s for a lot of things—where people believe that getting most of the way toward something is enough. So somebody says to this guy, “Hey, you made partner. Isn’t it time to buy a $20,000 watch?” And then the guy next to him goes, “You can buy a $400 watch that looks just as good as a $20,000 watch.” And this guy goes, “Great.” And that’s it—that’s as far as they go.

“Too many” is the answer to how many watches I have. But most of what is in my collection that’s important to me are watches that are not [necessarily] of significant financial value. I have a watch that belonged to each of my grandfathers that I had restored. And I did not have fancy grandfathers. These are watches that cost more to restore than they were worth, but are of incredible value to me. And a couple of my friends who I’ve worked with many, many times, my friends and mentors in movies have given me watches, and those are important to me because of that, because of where they came from and what they mean and the consideration that went into them.

Watches like Benrus, which is, again, not a Rolex-level name, but Benjamin Lazarus founded that company in New York, and that means something to me as a guy from New York. So there’s something significant there. There are a lot of newer watches that I’m fascinated with, whether it’s companies like Oris or smaller brands like Haven or Bernhardt, which I appreciate.

I mean, listen, I don’t own an Omega Speedmaster. I’d love to own a Speedmaster. I love what they’re doing with modern watches now, actually. I’d love to own a gold Rolex. I think there’s something really cool about a gold Rolex.

I don’t know what I would do if I had a Rolex 6542, a Bakelite Bezel GMT [from the ’50s], because those are the coolest-looking watches. But if you sneeze at it wrong, does the bezel crack? I can’t worry about that.

Yeah, and I don’t believe in that! I want to wear my watches.

#6733. 22 Designer Handbags That Will Stand the Test of Time

Few fashion purchases carry as much weight, both literally and financially, as a designer handbag. The right one can make an outfit, become a daily fixture on morning commutes, and, in some cases, retain its value long after checkout. But in a market where a new It bag seems to emerge every season (or with every scroll through your feed), figuring out which styles are worth the splurge isn't always straightforward.

Fashion history offers clues to sound investments. Some of today’s most coveted bags have been around for decades: Gucci’s Jackie traces its roots to the 1960s, while Dior’s Lady Dior became an icon of ’90s style thanks to Princess Diana. Fendi’s Baguette, meanwhile, outlived its early-aughts It-bag heyday and found a new generation of fans more than two decades later. Their enduring appeal speaks to the power of great design, which can transcend changing tastes, evolving trends, and creative director shake-ups.

Of course, a handbag doesn’t need decades of history behind it to become a wardrobe staple. Sometimes, an unexpected silhouette, celebrity endorsement, or clever design detail can turn a newcomer into a cult classic overnight. Identifying the forever pieces among today’s endless stream of new arrivals is then part of the fun.

Beyond the initial buzz, the most promising designs have some things in common: practical proportions, distinctive details, and versatility—all the more important when you’re considering a four-figure purchase. The best designer handbags should fit seamlessly into your wardrobe rather than demand an entirely new one. They should be flexible enough to carry everywhere from dinner to work and the grocery store, beautifully crafted to withstand years of wear, and stylish enough to elevate even the simplest of outfits.

Below, Vogue’s guide to the best designer handbags, from bona fide icons to established favorites and newer arrivals with the potential to become tomorrow’s most treasured pieces. Whether you're drawn to a heritage house signature or something less ubiquitous, these are the bags worth getting to know—and keeping close for years to come.

The Paddington was the bag of the mid-2000s, instantly recognizable for its slouchy shape and oversized padlock hardware. Worn by every It-girl from Kate Moss to Sienna Miller, it defined an era of bohemian glamour. In 2025, the cult bag returned under Chloé creative director Chemena Kamali, who has revived the padlock-topped icon in various sizes and colors.

Balenciaga’s Le City bag was a favorite of Noughties It-girls—think the Olsen twins, Nicole Richie, and Lindsay Lohan. It made a full-fledged comeback in 2024 with refreshed proportions and multiple colorways. Today, the archival icon endures as a house staple—equally tempting in its new iterations as vintage styles. While plenty of fashion lovers are reaching for the new model, which comes in a range of colorways, others, including British Vogue’s Naomi Smart, are securing their wishlist pieces second-hand on preloved sites such as eBay and Vinted.

Gucci’s Jackie is one of fashion’s true icons. Originally beloved by Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, the hobo-shaped shoulder bag has been reissued countless times, each wave balancing retro charm with contemporary relevance. Modern versions—sleek, compact, and available in lush hues, as well as go-with-everything neutrals—make it just as covetable today as in the ’60s.

First introduced as Jonathan Anderson’s debut bag at Loewe, the Puzzle quickly became a fashion-insider favorite for its origami-like panels and clever, shape-shifting construction. Now, with Proenza Schouler founders Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez as Loewe’s creative directors, the Puzzle remains a house cornerstone—offered in multiple sizes and colorways, with the classic full-size in black or beige still the chicest bet.

Miu Miu’s Aventure may feel in step with fashion’s current appetite for ladylike top handles, but the bag’s roots go back. Introduced for fall 2024, the softly structured style reimagines a doctor bag from the 2009 archives, complete with curved lines, a snap-hook closure, and vintage appeal. Since its debut, the Aventure has become one of Miu Miu’s most popular styles, offered in everything from nappa leather to suede and an ever-changing lineup of colors.

The Prada Passage bag may have only made its debut on the spring 2026 runway, but its architectural, slightly off-kilter silhouette already has the makings of a modern classic. The elongated style plays with contrasting textures and a clever bag-within-a-bag effect. With its folded sides, protruding flap, and slender handles, it’s practical, minimal, and guaranteed to become a must-have for collectors of the brand.

The Row has a knack for transforming familiar handbag silhouettes into instant must-haves, and the Agnes is no exception. Inspired by vintage bowling bags, the structured top handle is marked by its gently curved shape, tubular handles, flat base, and sweeping zip closure. Devoid of flashy logos or hardware, the Agnes features a quietly distinctive design that sets it apart—and feels destined to get even better with age.

Khaite is renowned for its arsenal of timeless, investment-worthy accessories. The brand's Blake bag reimagines the classic box silhouette with a softly structured, flap-front shape that combines clean lines with sculptural curves. The result is a contemporary crossbody that offers form and function. More recent Soft Blake styles loosen things up, translating the same understated elegance into a supple, slouchier shape designed for everyday wear.

Spotted on just about every cool girl, the Balenciaga Rodeo has quickly become one of fashion's defining It bags. Its slouchy silhouette draws inspiration from vintage briefcases, while a structured top handle and removable, adjustable leather strap allow it to be carried by hand, over the shoulder, or crossbody.

It was clear that the Empire bag was an instant hit upon walking into the Vogue offices—you can spot at least three perched on an editor’s desk at any given time. The appeal of this popular Coach style lies in its marriage of aesthetic and accessibility—its roomy design and mid-level price make it hard to ignore. Opt for the larger 40 model for daytime and the slightly more compact 35 for evenings.

First introduced in 2004 under then-creative director Tomas Maier, Bottega Veneta's Campana bag has been relaunched for fall 2025. The softly curved shoulder bag retains its signature Intrecciato weave and double handles, now with even sleeker lines. Its spacious silhouette and lack of hardware make it an effortless everyday option, while its two-decade history proves that some designs are timeless for a reason.

When Carrie Bradshaw slung a whipstitched Fendi baguette over her shoulder in Sex and The City, she helped turn the already-iconic bag into a worldwide sensation. And while the style has never really gone away, it has enjoyed a serious renaissance over the last decade, with a new generation discovering its Noughties charm. Recent re-editions, from tactile pony hair to richly embellished iterations, prove there’s still plenty of life left in the silhouette.

Originally introduced in the 1970s, Loewe's Amazona bag returned from the archives to mark the house's 180th anniversary. This medium-sized version is crafted in Spain from supple leather and finished with reinforced corners for added structure. True to its effortless appeal, it's designed to be carried slightly open—what Jonathan Anderson described as looking "like a chic mistake"—while a concealed closure keeps the contents secure. Removable shoulder and crossbody straps add to its versatility.

When Toteme introduced the T-Lock in 2022, the Swedish label proved its minimalist sensibility translated just as well to accessories as to ready-to-wear. Defined by a softly structured silhouette, curved flap, and instantly recognizable T-shaped clasp, the bag has since become a signature of the brand—and a favorite of celebrities like Katie Holmes. Available in everything from buttery leather to earthy suede, and in a range of sizes and colors, the T-Lock feels just as relevant today as it did four years ago—and promises to remain so for decades to come.

Saint Laurent’s Le 5 à 7 has become one of the house’s quintessential everyday bags, offered in both a sleek, subtly curved shoulder silhouette and a more spacious bucket shape. Its name nods to the Parisian “after-work to before-dinner” window, telegraphing day-to-night ease. Available in smooth or grained leather, suede, and seasonal finishes, both styles are discreet staples that read polished without trying.

Another iconic bag named after another iconic woman, Dior’s Lady Dior bag owes its fame to Princess Diana. Originally called the Chouchou, the boxy top-handle bag was gifted to Diana by then-First Lady of France, Bernadette Chirac, in September 1995. The princess quickly made it a signature, carrying it frequently to public engagements and requesting a version in blue to match her eyes. In 1996, Dior renamed the bag the Lady Dior in honor of its most famous fan. It remains one of the brand’s most popular bags.

Named for—and inspired by—the curved shape of its namesake French pastry, Lemaire’s Croissant has quickly become one of the house’s signatures. Curved panels give the crescent bag its memorable shape, allowing it to mold against the body when worn crossbody, while knotted strap ends and a looped zipper pull make for recognizable, playful finishes. Since launch, the line has expanded to include a variety of sizes and colorways.

Louis Vuitton’s Neverfull tote is often spotted on the arms of airport-bound celebrities, no doubt thanks to its practical, capacious interior (the clue is in the name) and timeless logo leather design. Introduced in 2007 as a beach bag, the style has experienced a revival in recent years.

Launched in the fall/winter 2022 collection, Miu Miu’s Wander bag has already secured its place in the designer bag hall of fame, thanks to its distinctive matelassé detailing and compact size. Beloved by the likes of Emma Corrin, Alexa Chung, Gigi Hadid, Hailey Bieber and Jaime Xie, to name but a few, its star shows no sign of fading.

Fashion-insider favorite accessories brand Savette built its name on retro-tinged ladylike handbags, but the Soft Symmetry takes the label’s codes in a more relaxed direction. Introduced in 2026, the roomy top handle trades the original Symmetry’s structure for a slouchier silhouette, generous interior, and dangling zipper tails that lend it an appealingly undone quality. Founder Amy Zurek designed it with longevity in mind: recognizable enough to feel distinctly Savette, but restrained enough to transcend a trend cycle.

Leave it to Prada to turn a humble, dust bag-like drawstring pouch into one of 2026’s most coveted accessories. Introduced on the spring 2026 runway, the Wish Pouch’s pared-back construction takes on a different look depending on the material: Silk duchesse versions come in jewel-box shades, while leather, nylon, and neutral iterations offer a more understated take on the whimsical silhouette.

Coach knows its way around a buzzy bag (see: the Bella Hadid-beloved Brooklyn), and Chelsea is already emerging as another hit. The roomy shoulder bag pairs a relaxed, soft shape with a flap closure and minimal hardware. Available in leather and suede, it has the easy, throw-it-over-your-shoulder appeal that makes a bag more likely to become a wardrobe mainstay than a one-season wonder.

Well, it shifts from season to season. For fall 2026, Prada is back on top: The Lyst Index crowned it the world’s hottest brand in Q3, with the house reclaiming the number one spot for the first time since 2023. Elsewhere, Gucci remained in the top five, Chloé climbed two places, and Bottega Veneta rose three spots following Louise Trotter’s much-anticipated debut for the house.

The season’s most-wanted bags offer an equally varied snapshot of what shoppers want right now. Prada’s silk duchesse Wish Pouch was Lyst’s hottest product of Q3, with searches surging 498 percent. Meanwhile, Balenciaga’s slouchy Rodeo landed at number eight, with the fashion platform calling out “a spectrum of slouchy top-handle bags” among the quarter’s strongest performers.

It bags like Toteme’s T-Lock Bag and Miu Miu’s Aventure have proved they have staying power beyond their initial buzz, while perennial signatures, including Saint Laurent’s Le 5 à 7 and Gucci’s Jackie, continue to make the case for investing in a silhouette with history behind it. At the same time, a new class of contenders is emerging: Savette has softened its signature polish with the relaxed Soft Symmetry, and The Row has put its typically minimalist spin on the vintage bowling bag with the Agnes.

The takeaway? There isn’t one handbag (or even one handbag aesthetic) dominating right now. The most compelling styles range from softly slouching carryalls to structured top handles and fanciful evening pouches. So ultimately, the smartest investment is the bag that works with your wardrobe and your life—and that you’ll still want to carry long after its moment on the Lyst Index has passed.

#6732. Shooting Matt Damon in the Desert and Leaning Into Discomfort

It was a beautiful day to be indoors. In barren Lancaster, California, the temperature had hit the mid-90s, and the feels-like figure in my weather app topped triple digits. We were professional. We were stoic. But at a certain point, you just give in to the heat of the desert. At a certain point, you wilt a little.

Matt Damon, mercifully, never did. Damon may be the least-debated pick in GQ Men of the Year history—he’s still riding the billion-dollar wave of The Odyssey, one of the great cinematic accomplishments this century. Damon was also, by some distance, the most unbothered man on that desert set, and all while being the only one wearing heavenly black tailoring (a peak-lapel Norton & Sons jacket, and glorious mohair Celine pants). It was Bourne-esque. Odyssean, even! Three decades into being a film star, Damon has familiarity with endurance, both creative and literal. In his cover story, he walks our Frazier Tharpe through the physical cost of making Christopher Nolan’s epic, up to and including a night in Scotland on which he didn’t sleep at all. The piece is a portrait of a movie star who still treats the job as a job, most of all when it is inconvenient, unfair, or uncomfortable.

Discomfort has been something of a theme for me this year. I will confess that I knew 2026 would be an administrative ordeal from the moment I accepted this new role at GQ. There was a move from London to New York (including a cat, whose opinion was not consulted). There was a home to find. And there was the discovery that the land of the free has impressive disdain for a grown man with no credit score. None of it was enjoyable. All of it, I think, is good for me.

I have the good fortune to work with many brilliant editors and writers. A recurring note I like to give is: Where is the tension? Without tension, there’s no story. I am not a confrontational person, but I find confrontation on the page irresistible. I want you to stumble, in every issue of GQ, onto something uncomfortable, or uncomfortably new. A magazine that agrees with you from cover to cover is a magazine that you have already read. And I would hate to do that to you.

This issue does not let you off lightly. After some life advice from an honest-to-God astronaut who went deeper into space than anyone that’s ever lived, you’ll read about Chris Rock’s unvarnished thoughts on divorce, discomfort, and reclamation, and Andrew Garfield’s very real anxieties in playing Sam Altman, the complicated man who’s been described as the Oppenheimer of our time. From there, we hang out with the men risking the unknown to get hot on peptides, which is, for better or worse, the defining male-vanity story of 2026.

A few months ago I started putting my email address in these letters (adam@gq.com). You’ve been generous. You’ve been thoughtful. A handful of you have been unhinged. But one note showed up way more than I thought it would: NO POLITICS, PLEASE.

I understand the impulse. I know These Modern Times are stressful, and wouldn’t it be nice if GQ were a place of apolitical tranquility? Alas. GQ has always taken men seriously as full human beings, and full human beings can handle tough conversations, opposing viewpoints, and a little gray area. There’s nothing noble about steering clear of the uncomfortable.

Which brings me to our special package on Cornell, anchored by a dispatch from campus by Savannah Sobrevilla. It is about an alleged sexual assault. It is also about the men on the sidelines of sexual assault. Some of the young men we meet through the story are students who are earnestly and inelegantly trying to grapple with how serious the alleged crimes are, with the crude and cruel culture that surrounds them, and with what role, exactly, they play in exacerbating that culture—or could play in diminishing it. It’s not easy reading, but not everything should be. ✦

#6730. I Wear-Tested En Route’s Viral, Under-$50 Jewelry—Now I Get Why My Favorite Celebs Love It

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Shop the pieces worn by Bella Hadid, Lola Tung, and Doechii.

What do Bella Hadid, Doechii, Camila Cabello, and Lola Tung all have in common? They’re all known for killing it on the carpet, yes—but once the cameras went down, I took notice that they’ve each been wearing the same under-$100 jewelry brand.

It might surprise you that some of the biggest stars in entertainment are wearing budget-friendly baubles. But after adding a few choice accessories from the brand to my own collection, I have to admit: En Route has some of the trendiest, most compliment-garnering jewelry the internet has to offer. (And, let’s face it: it doesn’t hurt that it costs less than the price of my favorite takeout.)

Ahead, I’m giving my honest review on En Route’s most popular pieces after months of wear-testing in my everyday jewelry rotation. Keep reading for the rundown on this viral, celebrity-loved brand—including the affordable pieces I think are worth it.

As an editor who’s been covering jewelry trends for years, I’ll admit that I was a bit skeptical when I saw the price tag. In my experience, $30 jewelry either (A) turns your skin a sickly shade of green, or (B) tarnishes to an unbecoming rust color in a matter of weeks. That’s why I wanted to put En Route’s pieces to the test. I wore them to work, regularly washed my hands with them, kept them on for sweaty outdoor runs while marathon training, and even accidentally showered in them a time or two. (Ya know, the normal wear and tear that your jewelry is going to experience throughout its lifetime.)

The brand claims its jewelry is hypoallergenic, meaning that it’s lead- and nickel-free and should be safe for shoppers with sensitive skin. Its gold-plated jewelry is also three times thicker than industry standard, according to its FAQ section, which means it’s designed to last longer than competing budget brands—a claim I was excited to put to the test.

Without spoiling my full review, here’s the TL;DR: if you want to shop trendy, unique pieces that show off your personal style, you should be running to add En Route to your collection.

Before we dive in, it’s worth noting that all of En Route’s jewelry is gold-plated—not solid gold. What does this mean? The base of the jewelry is made from an inexpensive metal, like brass or stainless steel, and then a very thin layer of gold is electroplated on top. This gives the look of real gold without the price tag.

As you might expect, gold-plated jewelry isn’t nearly as long-lasting as solid gold and silver; the thin layer will eventually rub off, particularly on jewelry like rings or bracelets that receive a lot of wear and tear. In my experience, standard gold-plated jewelry will begin fading or tarnishing within one to three years.

To ensure the longevity of your jewelry, En Route recommends avoiding water and chemicals like makeup or perfume (though showering every once in a while is A-okay)—and they even have an entire section of their site for waterproof jewelry that’s safe to get wet.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that I receive at least one compliment every time I wear one of my necklaces from En Route. Over the summer, I found myself reaching for the Infinity Choker almost every day, since its colorful beads glimmer in the sunshine and look great with a simple white tank top or sundress. These days, I’m spicing up turtlenecks and basic tees with this vintage-inspired collar necklace that looks like a family heirloom but costs less than $40.

After several months of frequent wear, both of my picks have held up without so much as a smudge. Just note that neither is advertised as being waterproof, so I’d definitely avoid wearing them in the shower or during a workout to keep them looking shiny and new for as long as possible.

Upon first glance, I was immediately impressed by how unique En Route’s ring selection is—and after testing them for a few months, I’ve become even more of a fan. The selection is basically perfect if you’re looking to shop personality-driven pieces that express your unique style. Take Bella Hadid, for example. The star was spotted doubling up with the Wonder Pearl ring on multiple fingers, showing off the chunky sculptural bezel and a pretty faux pearl inside. Or, consider Lola Tung’s stack of hammered silver rings—a master class in simple yet effective ring stacking.

I, on the other hand, found myself enamored by the Mojave Buckle ring. It runs a little bit small, but I love the subtle Western flair it adds to any look. The brand recommends keeping its rings out of water as much as possible, but even with regular hand-washing, I haven’t noticed any tarnishing or fading so far.

As someone with multiple piercings, I’m here to tell you that you can never have too many earrings. The greatest perk I found while testing En Route’s earring selection is just how lightweight they are—which is essential if you want to be comfortable all day and avoid stretching out your piercings. Despite sturdy-looking shapes and ornate details, the earrings I tested were feather-light and virtually unnoticeable all day long.

Possibly my favorite jewelry piece I tested from the brand were these Star earrings. They garnered multiple compliments from friends and strangers alike, and people were shocked when I told them they cost just $22. What’s more, the stainless steel material doesn’t irritate my ears and this pair just so happens to be waterproof.

Bella Hadid wearing the Silent Drop earrings in gold.

Lola Tung wearing the Clio earrings in silver.

My only word of caution: while the earrings look expensive, their lightweight construction makes them feel a little cheap in your hands. This isn’t a dealbreaker for me since they’ve held up flawlessly so far, but don’t expect them to have the same heft and quality of your pricey solid gold studs.

I’m not a big bracelet person. There’s something about the feeling of jewelry sliding and clanking around on my wrists that really bothers me—so it’s a rare occasion when I decide to put one on. But for the sake of this review, I tested the Athena bracelet and the Harmonic Hour watch, and honestly? I kinda loved them.

While I’m still not a fan of the clinking feeling, I loved the colored gemstone details that glittered in direct light and added a cool-girl flair with virtually zero effort. The lightweight construction makes them almost unnoticeable throughout the day, so I didn’t notice them as much as hefty bangles. Bonus points for the fact that they’re pretty easy to put on and take off by yourself, since they have simple clasps and T-bar closures. There’s even body jewelry and hand chains for more ways to personalize your jewelry stack.

After several months of constant wear-testing, I’m convinced: En Route is one of the best affordable jewelry brands on the market if you’re looking for cute, trendy, and personality-driven pieces. The wide selection of options—ranging from chunky statement pieces to wearable basics in both gold and silver—makes it super easy to express your personal style without dropping hundreds of dollars.

For shoppers with sensitive skin, I love that everything is hypoallergenic, according to the brand, so you don’t have to worry as much about how your skin will react to your new affordable jewelry. And while not everything is designed to hold up in water, I love that there’s a dedicated section on the website for shopping waterproof pieces. Even the rings, earrings, and necklaces I tested held up well with occasional splashes and frequent hand-washing.

En Route’s overall quality for the price is one of the best I’ve seen. That said, if you’re looking for investment-worthy jewelry you can wear literally 24/7—as in, at the gym, in the shower, or to sleep—I’d recommend investing in a longer-lasting (albeit more expensive) premium metal option. Nearly everything onsite is gold- or rhodium-plated, so they’ll likely start tarnishing within a couple of years, unlike pricier vermeil or solid gold and silver pieces.

Samantha Jones is a senior shopping editor at Hearst Magazines, where she specializes in style, wellness, and home content. #6728. Are Young Men the New Kings of the Swing Vote?

Two years ago, it seemed that the young men of Gen Z were shaping up to be hardcore conservatives. More than half of them voted for Donald Trump’s second presidency, refuting the idea that young people tend to lean progressive. Liberal media panicked about finding “a Joe Rogan of the left” who could reach them, and conservatives took a victory lap. “Gen Z Has Turned Right!” Fox News’s Greg Gutfeld announced, citing a report from the Harvard Kennedy School that highlighted, among other insights, the ways social media has led to an increase in conservatism among young folks. A Turning Point USA Poll from around the same time declared Generation Z “the most conservative generation in decades.”

On Tuesday night, though, as a blue tidal wave flipped states from Iowa to Texas, it was young men who comprised a critical segment of the new Democratic coalition. As reported by CIRCLE, a non-partisan research organization at Tufts University, white men between the ages of 18 to 29 voted blue by a 10-point margin; in 2024, exit polling indicated that 56% of all young men voted for Donald Trump. Even more remarkably, young people across the board voted for Democratic congressional candidates by a 40% margin, according to data from NBC.

“In the wake of 2024, there was this whole catastrophizing panic,” says Aidan Kohn-Murphy, the founder of Gen Z for Change (formerly known as TikTok for Biden) and a prominent political influencer. “Oh my God, everything we thought about Gen Z is wrong. It's actually a conservative generation. And no, that's not what was happening. I mean, a huge part of Gen Z just didn't show up to vote because they didn't feel like they had a reason.”

For Democratic strategist Eric Stern, connecting with men on an emotional level was critical in getting them out to vote. Stern has worked on Ruben Gallego and John Fetterman’s campaigns; his political ad agency, FIGHT, has produced spots for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Senator-Elect Abdul El-Sayed, and Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa, to name a few. This election cycle, Stern sought to change voters’ perception of what a Democrat can look like.

“Our most notable ad of the general election was Bob [Brooks] standing in front of a literal dumpster fire and then putting it out because he's a firefighter,” he said. Brooks, now the Representative-elect in the Lehigh Valley, flipped his seat on Tuesday. “A ton of Latino men are really into boxing and MMA fighting, and so Ruben [Gallego] held events around boxing,” Stern told me. For Texas’ Hinojosa, who'll become the state’s first Democratic governor in 35 years when she's sworn in in January, that meant running an ad during Mexican boxing champion Canelo Álvarez's match against Christian Mbilli, an event with a massive Latino viewing audience.

Still, Kohn-Murphy and Stern both argued that the main issue on the ballot this cycle was affordability. “If you look at polling, far and away the top issue for voters is cost of living,” Stern said. “And so you can run a million ads saying that ‘Jane Doe is for they/them,’ but it's not going to resonate with people in the same way if they can't afford to keep their lights on.”

When I asked Republican political consultant Kirsten Kukowski about young men voting blue, she brought up affordability too. After all, nearly nine months into the Iran War, a barrel of oil still costs $100. “Men and young men voted with their bank accounts,” she offered. “And for the last several years, that's how they've been voting. And I think that's how Donald Trump won that group two years ago, because he was talking about affordability and inflation.”

Kukowski, the former Communications Director for the Republican National Committee, now runs her own firm, K2 and Company, out of Minneapolis. “At some point here, people expect results,” she continued. “People expected results from Donald Trump, and they didn't see that. So now we're on the clock again for another two years.”

#6727. Everything We Know About ‘Black Doves’ Season 3

Black Doves, the sleek and sexy Netflix series about the complicated friendship between a spy played by Keira Knightley and an assassin played by Ben Whishaw, has returned for season 2. Already caught up? Not sure whether the long-term commitment is worth it? Here’s what we know about the odds that Black Doves will be renewed for season 3.

The first season brought Knightley’s character Helen, a spy married to a prominent conservative politician, back into action in the aftermath of her lover’s murder. The second season shoves her into the spotlight as her husband becomes prime minister. Meanwhile, in both seasons, Whishaw’s character Sam does his best to protect her while fighting his own demons, internally and externally. As various secret organizations and powers that be pull their strings to use them as pawns, the two of them can really only trust each other.

As of the season 2 release, Black Doves has not yet been renewed for season 3. The second season was announced before the first season dropped on Netflix. In theory, that’s concerning. But maybe the show was initially “ordered” for two seasons, and they announced it as an early renewal to create some well-deserved buzz before the premiere.

So far, season 2 reviews have been good. If the audiences follow, then we should (hopefully) get the good news soon.

No spoilers, but season 2 leaves a lot up in the air. Many of the characters are split up. Big secrets have been revealed. I wouldn’t be surprised if a third season went international again. Every story about a spy and/or assassin teaches us that you can’t escape your past.

However, since Black Doves is not based on a preexisting book series or film, it is difficult to decipher what happens next. That’s up to creator Joe Barton, who of course also created The Lazarus Project and recently adapted the play Amadeus to the small screen.

This is the thing. There were two years between Black Doves season 1 and season 2. That’s the problem with getting big movie stars to make television shows. Scheduling can be difficult.

But are we really going to have to wait until 2028 for Black Doves season 3? That would not be ideal. With all of the twists and turns of a show like this, you’ll need to do a total preseason series rewatch to remember what happened. If it is 2028, it’ll probably drop in November or December. That’s the one thing you can count on...this is a chilly series.

#6725. Ralph Lauren Pre-Fall 2027

Ralph Lauren picked up the Menswear Designer of the Year Award at the CFDAs earlier this week. He also took home the organization’s first men’s prize in 1981. That means—if I have my dates right—he’s been at the top of American fashion since before this year’s other winners were born. In an industry built on change, renewing and maintaining a legacy can be as difficult as building one, but even as he approaches the brand’s 60th anniversary, Lauren still has fashion’s attention. PoloFest, the vintage marketplace the company organized in Tokyo last month, with its 5,000 specially selected archival Polo pieces and 10,000 visitors, is bound to spawn imitators across the business.

This pre-fall collection wasn’t designed to make that kind of noise, but it’s as rooted in the brand’s iconography as anything else it does. Take the glen plaid pantsuit in look 3—it’s based on a suit that Lauren himself frequently wears and made by tailors in Italy with the specialized techniques that give men’s suiting its sharp lines and structure. The track pants in look 1 are another Ralph tic; he’s always liked mixing casual and formal, low and high. Purple is the accent color here this season, as it is across so much of fashion, alongside minty green, though we can’t blame the prevailing currents. Lauren pays no heed to trends. Case in point: The silvery plunge-front halter top is a lift from his own 1990s archives.

#6723. What Really Happened Between Sarah and John That Caused Their Divorce After ‘Love Is Blind’? A Much-Needed and Very Shocking Update

Love Is Blind Season 11 didn’t exactly go as planned for most of the engaged couples, with pretty much everyone breaking up before saying “I do.” But one pair managed to pull through! Sarah and John exchanged vows and got married (legally, I might add) during the Love Is Blind season finale.

“You are beautiful, you are brilliant, you are thoughtful, and I love you,” John said in his vows, while Sarah gushed “I love that you are sensitive and considerate and I find you funny.” Honestly, it was sweet!

The thing is...this finale was filmed over a year ago. Meaning, we’re in desperate need of an update on where Sarah and John stand today. Enter: the reunion! Netflix filmed the Love Is Blind reunion pretty recently, and there’s a shocking update on Sarah and John.

During an early reunion viewing on Tudum, John revealed he had an emotional affair about a year into the marriage, which led to their separation. "Unfortunately Sarah and I are no longer together, which is my fault,” John said. “We had a wonderful year of marriage, the two of us. Shared a lot of memories together. We had a wonderful year of marriage together, but unfortunately I made a mistake and there was a major breach of trust on my part. It's hard to talk about. There was a boys’ night I went on with a bunch of my friends and I just acted un-husbandly.”

He added that “nothing physical happened," and when pressed said “I texted one of the people we met out that night, and nothing happened, but she saw the texts and they were inappropriate for me to be sending as her husband. It was like three [texts], but they were bad.”

As for Sarah, she said the situation was “very sad,” that she'd struggled with “how John spoke to me” in the marriage, and that his behavior on the “boys’ night” was the "final thing that made me want to leave."

We don’t have information on where Sarah and John stand circa this moment, but it seems safe to assume they aren’t about to get back together given how the relationship ended.

#6721. 13 Rugby Shirts Under $150 for Credible Old-Money Cosplay

Historically, rugby shirts are a somewhat conflicted character in the never-ending tale of menswear shirting. On one hand, they’re a prep staple on par with OCBDs, loafers, and boat shoes. On the other hand, they were quite literally designed to handle the rigors of full-contact rugby and were later embraced by folks who proudly call themselves dirtbags.

There’s an interesting duality to rugby shirts: they can feel twee or they can feel traditionally sporty. Thanks to this polarity, it makes it even easier to fit into your wardrobe. Regardless of which camp you fall in, rugby’s crush. And thanks to a recent resurgence, we thought it would be a good idea to highlight some rugby shirts under $150.

Not only are they traditionally as comfortable as any polo you own, they’re also refined enough to take into stuffier settings, rugged enough to handle some serious outdoor exploration and flexible enough to wear from Friday to Monday morning (but don’t do that, probably). And while we love an expensive version of, well, anything, we also love it when we can find some killer alternatives for prices we’d like to think of as reasonable. There wasn’t a paucity of options either, so we rounded up 13 of our favorites, right below.

One of the least expensive options on this list is also one of the best—the loose, shorter cut makes wearing it with jeans, some chinos or virtually anything else in your closet as easy as any polo you have in the arsenal.

J.Crew has a few louder options in the catalog, but the pared-down, solid-bodied iterations are even more affordable and play a supporting role with as much skill and charisma as your favorite character actor.

There is an actual science to color combinations, and Gramicci deserves an Einstein Award for this one.

When done right, a rugby can be one of the best outdoors shirts on the market, and this one is just that: super comfortable, a little hardy and delightfully reminiscent of the ones you would've seen in Camp 4.

There's simply no way that the company founded by an original Camp 4 denizen could ever make a rugby not worthy of a Half Dome assault, and it's also improbably still under $150.

Alex Mill makes a few killer monochromatic, garment-dyed variations of this striped number, but this one is more fun than those and we could all use a little bit of fun when the days are as short as they are now.

It's odd to call something a rugby if it doesn't have a contrasting placket, but this one gets a pass because everything else checks out and it's also made out of a hardy-ass jersey fabric.

One of the best rugby shirts we've found also happens to meet the rigorous price qualifications of this list—and now it's half-off—and it's not all that often that the best of anything is also a value play.

Putting "Iconic" in the name is one of those things that can backfire on you if it doesn't live up to the billing, but this one does and remains both a standard of the genre and, against all odds, under $150.

Very few brands appreciate the rugby—or the possibilities that exist under the rugby banner— more than 18 East, and not only is the Harold reimagining the notion of stripe spacing within the genre, but it's also the only short-sleeve option on this list.

This one is going to keep working its way into lists as long as its available because sometimes a brand just nails it. In this case, the cocktail of perfectly-faded brown and black is radiating Leatherheads (complimentary) and the cut is the comfy kind that can layer on either side.

Some big ol' stripes, a woven collar and a cool little oxford cloth hit at the inside of the neck are just a few details elevating this one from "not bad" to "oh hell yeah." (It's also on sale, which always helps.)

Hear me out: I've made a habit of finding stuff in the women's section that fits better than anything on the men's side, and this rugby has all the trademark elements of those past hitters. Also, it might be the softest one on this whole list.

#6716. Nicole Kidman Celebrates the Art of Ballet in a Voluminous Chanel Tutu

She made her LACMA Gala debut in a messy high ponytail

Every year, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art welcomes the art, film, fashion, and entertainment industries to its annual fundraising event. Since its inception back in 2011, the Art+Film Gala, as it is known, has become a staple fixture on the fall calendar, seeing everyone from models to actors to philanthropists to musicians to athletes return time and time again. But this year, the starry festivities also saw a new face or two—including the one and only Nicole Kidman.

Making her LACMA debut, Kidman showed up to the event wearing a voluminous Chanel dress from Matthieu Blazy’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection. On top, the taupe-and-cream piece featured a long-sleeve corset bodice, with a raw-edge neckline that contrasted the structured boning below. From the hips, layers and layers of semi-sheer tulle cut at different lengths created a high-low tutu skirt that, even when still, gave the illusion of movement.

Before heading inside, the Babygirl actor—with a messy high ponytail and open-toe heels—stopped for photos by Chris Burden’s Urban Light art installation, which doubled as a red carpet for the evening. She was joined by the likes of Alex Consani, Kim Kardashian, and Paris Hilton.

LACMA’s annual gala was founded to support the museum’s efforts to expand its programming, making film more central to its exhibitions and education. It has placed a focus on the intersection of art and film, and takes a moment each year to celebrate individuals for their contributions to the visual and cinematic arts. Tonight, it honored the work of painter Vija Celmins, known for her photo-realistic explorations of nature, as well as Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. Blackpink’s Rosé was tapped for a musical performance, and, for the 15th year, Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow served as co-chairs.

#6711. Kim Kardashian Returns to the LACMA Gala in Burgundy Gucci Sequins

Her turtleneck dress dipped dangerously low in the back

Kim Kardashian is back at the LACMA Art+Film Gala. A frequent staple of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art’s annual fundraising event, the reality star returned to the famed street-lamp installation (Chris Burden’s Urban Light) in a shimmering burgundy dress, joining fellow attendees such as Alex Consani, Kylie Jenner, Nicole Kidman, and Paris Hilton.

Courtesy of Gucci, the event’s sponsor, Kardashian’s floor-sweeping sequin look was at once modest and revealing—with long sleeves and a turtleneck bodice contrasted by side cutouts and an open back. The All’s Fair star gave the look a moody, smokey-eye glam, long tousled hair, and a color-matched manicure.

Welcoming everyone from models to actors to philanthropists to musicians to athletes, the gala celebrated its 15th year this evening, supporting its ongoing efforts to expand its film programming. And like every year, it was co-chaired by Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow. It honored the work of painter Vija Celmins, known for her photo-realistic work that explores the complexity of nature, as well as Dune filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. Blackpink’s Rosé was tapped for a musical performance.

Kardashian first attended the Art+Film Gala over a decade ago, showing up to the 2014 edition with Kanye West. And the next year, just one month before the couple welcomed son Saint West, she made her sophomore appearance in a sheer black dress that highlighted her baby bump. The Skims founder continued to support the museum, finding time for the fundraiser in 2017, 2018, 2022, 2023, and 2024.
