#6672. Black Nails: The Little Black Manicure Is Having a Major Moment

A slick of jet-black nail polish never goes out of style, and is equal to more than the sum of its parts. It can read grungy, or glam, as a surprisingly versatile shade; and now the inky manicure is enjoying a run as fall’s chicest nail trend. Forget elaborate nail art, milky neutrals, or even the season’s customary burgundy and Bordeaux, because Hailey Bieber, Dua Lipa, Kylie Jenner, and Selena Gomez have all been going back to black.

At the 2026 Academy Museum Gala, Bieber offered a particularly polished take on the trend, pairing her bubblegum-pink Chanel gown with glossy, jet-black nails. Her go-to nail artist, Zola Ganzorigt, used OPI Intelli-Gel in Black Onyx, shaping the nails into elongated almonds and finishing them with a lacquer-like shine. The jewel-black shade was a striking counterpoint to the sweetness of her dress—a glam goth moment—and a marked departure from the glazed, barely-there manicures that have become a Mrs. Hailey Bieber signature.

For others, black nails aren’t just a seasonal trend, but a regular fixture in their nail appointment calendar. Dua Lipa has long favored a midnight manicure, wearing the shade even in the height of summer, when brighter colors and fun decals typically reign supreme. Kylie Jenner, too, is a longtime devotee. At a Kylie Cosmetics holiday party, she paired glossy black almond-shaped nails with a frothy, feather-trimmed pink dress. Rather than adding a pop of color to a neutral outfit, both Jenner and Bieber made the case for doing the inverse, grounding a sugary look with something dark and decidedly cool.

Hailey Bieber’s glam goth manicure at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala.

There are plenty of ways to play with the formula, too. Selena Gomez has previously experimented with a black velvet manicure, courtesy of her longtime nail artist Tom Bachik, lending the otherwise simple shade a soft, light-catching dimension. Bachik used Chanel’s Le Vernis in Le Diable En Chanel; after meticulously shaping and prepping the nails, he applied the house’s La Base Camélia before layering on the deep, almost-black lacquer.

Selena Gomez’s “velvet noir” manicure, courtesy of Tom Bachik.

For the festive season, a dusting of chrome or a magnetic cat-eye finish can bring a little extra drama. Shape makes a difference, too: longer almond nails, as favored by Bieber and Jenner, feel sleek and glamorous, while shorter, squarer silhouettes offer a more understated, slightly punky alternative.

Part of black polish’s enduring appeal is that it works across skin tones, nail lengths, and personal styles—nail artist Julia Diogo even describes them as “winter nude.” It’s equally at home with a slouchy knit and jeans as it is with an outre dress, and has enough presence to make even the simplest outfit feel considered. And while there’s certainly room for embellishment, there’s something quite chic about keeping things so simple. No nail art, no glitter (yet!): just two coats of glossy noir.

#6671. Bob Dylan Just Dropped a 39-Disc Box Set. I Listened to Every Single One

It showed up in my inbox on a Tuesday afternoon without any particular fanfare, just an email from Legacy Recordings with a link to a stream. Artist: Bob Dylan. Title: Rolling Thunder Revue — The 1976 Live Recordings. Total Tracks: 381.

The link brought me to a bare-bones Sony Music web page, a couple light grey boxes arranged against a dark grey background. A small window in the middle of the page occupied maybe 10% of the available space. Inside the window were lines of text with lengthy, baroque file names, one on top of another. You could see about five at a time, starting with the first:

Bob Dylan_The Rolling Thunder Revue The 1976 Live Recordings_G0100060414779_01_01_Visions of Johanna_USSM12603067_CT122.

Bob Dylan_The Rolling Thunder Revue The 1976 Live Recordings_G0100060414779_01_02_If You See Her, Say Hello_USSM12603068_CT122.

This, it hardly needs to be said, is not the ideal way to familiarize yourself with the 31 hours and 18 minutes of new music included in the latest box set from Bob Dylan Industries. Like previous installments of the Live Recordings series, 1976 is an exhaustive accounting of (nearly) every second of (nearly) every show and concert given by Bob Dylan on a legendary tour. If a document of a performance from this tour exists, it is here, whether you want it or not.

There’s a certain thrill to a release like this, especially for the Dylan mujahideen, those of us willing to engage in the struggle. The 1976 Live Recordings is best thought of as a choose-your-own-adventure set, allowing you the opportunity to ramble along with the Rolling Thunder Revue at whatever pace you find comfortable. You can dip in on St. Petersburg (4/23/76) for the first recorded edition of “Idiot Wind,” then mosey on to Gainesville (4/25/76) for the only-ever performance of “Dink’s Song,” then settle in for a long date with Oklahoma City (5/18/76), one of the strongest complete shows. And if you want to summit the whole mountain—well, hit “play” on Lakeland (4/18/76) and let it rip. Just remember to stay hydrated.

As exciting as the sheer volume of new Bob Dylan music is, these ultra-complete tour retrospectives can be an intimidating listening experience. This is especially true in the case of The 1976 Live Recordings, which captures not the crackerjack bonhomie of the inaugural Rolling Thunder Revue, but the second, flabbier incarnation—halitosis and head scarves rather than whiteface and roses.

Dylan caught lightning in a bottle with the first Rolling Thunder, trucking around northeastern college towns with his ramshackle rock carnival while simultaneously 1) shooting an autofictional art film, and 2) trying to piece his broken marriage back together (partially by forcing his wife to act in said art film). The looks were immaculate, the vibes heady, the performances electric. Just peep a few minutes of a 1975 “Isis”—talk about the ghost of electricity howling in the bones of a face. The music press tailed the show from town to town throughout, breathlessly reporting on the latest feats of derring-do from Bob and co-conspirators. Rolling Thunder became a viral sensation, a meme, an object of FOMO decades before the term was invented.

For Dylan, it was the culmination of a thrilling 24-month period in which he’d returned to touring, recorded three brilliant albums, and reclaimed his reputation as the most vital force in rock songs. Taken together, Planet Waves, Blood On The Tracks, and Desire, along with the Before The Flood tour in ‘74 and Rolling Thunder in ‘75, seemed a clear statement of intent. You can’t repeat the past? Whaddya mean you can’t, of course you can.

Riding high on good will and good press, Bob got the band back together the following year. It was only natural. The first Rolling Thunder had been an experiment of sorts, a burst of creativity fueled in large part by spontaneity and esprit de corps. There was a real “let’s put on a show!” energy to the proceedings. Tour dates were announced only a few days in advance, the itinerary unfolding according to the whims of the man in the wide-brimmed hat, and concerts were given not in theaters, but in New England’s stuffiest gymnasia and rotary halls.

The mercurial, DIY approach was a big part of the magic, but it also limited the tour’s reach. The sequel would be a professional operation: fully produced, well-rehearsed, hosted in cavernous coliseums across the American South. Better, boozier, browner.

Those latter two descriptors certainly applied to Rolling Thunder ‘76. As for the former, it depends on who you ask. The energy of the ‘75 shows was dialed back considerably, the wiry charge dissipating somewhere between the action on stage and the tens of thousands in the stands. It would have been impossible to reproduce the energy of a room like Plymouth’s War Memorial Auditorium (capacity 1,500) in a place like Fort Collins’ Hughes Stadium (capacity 30,000), and Bob didn’t even try. Instead, he and the band dialed up the cream quotient, turning the sound into something thicker, a little less wild. If Rolling Thunder ‘75 was a bantamweight, dodging and dancing around the ring, ‘76 was a heavyweight—slower, steadier, with a brutal left hook.

Some of the best Desire cuts (“Hurricane,” “Sara”) were stripped from the ‘76 setlists, replaced with Blood On The Tracks material that neatly mapped the emotional geography of Dylan’s crumbling marriage. Most shows included some, if not all, of the following: “Tangled Up In Blue,” a tale of missed connections and cruel fate; “You’re A Big Girl Now,” a bitter, disillusioned sequel to “Positively 4th Street;” “Idiot Wind,” the breakup song to end all breakup songs, a kiss-off to both a former lover and a former self; and “You’re Gonna Make Me Lonesome When You Go,” a sweet little number written, not coincidentally, about the young A&R rep Bob had been seeing on the side. To the surprise of no one, Sara Dylan would file for divorce early the following year.

Listening now, it’s clear that the live Blood material is the lifeblood of Rolling Thunder ‘76. Bob is invested in these songs like they’re written in his soul: performances of “Idiot Wind” and “Shelter From The Storm” highlight every show in which they appear, and “Tangled” is always interesting, even if it’s occasionally more tuneless than it ought to be. The other stuff is more hit-and-miss.

Take the 4/22/76 taping for the Midnight Special television program, which notably lacks any Tracks tracks. Instead, Bob and company meander through an abbreviated selection of greatest hits in a vain attempt at pleasing the crowd (and, presumably, network execs hoping to sell ad spots against the programming). It’s the Dylan pupu platter: a few “protest” songs, a few mid-Sixties rockers, and a couple contemporary cuts as a sop to the actual fans present. Several Rolling Thunder cast members make appearances—Joan Baez, Bobby Neuwirth, Roger McGuinn—but no one’s heart seems to be in it. Dylan was dissatisfied with the results at the time, and he refused to allow the performance to air. Now here it is a half-century later, available for all of us to judge ourselves. Turns out Bob made the right call.

I can’t help but compare The 1976 Live Recordings to last year’s salvo from BD Industries, Through The Open Window: The Bootleg Series Vol. 18 1956-1963. That volume covered plenty of well-trod ground, tracing Bob’s earliest days in the Greenwich Village folk scene. Still, producers Sean Wilentz and Steve Berkowitz managed to string the collection’s hundred-odd tracks into something coherent and compelling. The result is a release that is intentional, engaging, and, despite its marathon length, essential.

The same cannot be said about this latest set. On a personal level, I find 1976 Bob much more compelling than I do 1962 Bob—I like my Dylan aged, like a fine Cabernet. But the experience of listening to The 1976 Live Recordings is somewhat less satisfying than that of Through The Open Window. Any time I return to Sony Music’s cursed promo portal, I feel like I’m pulling the lever of a slot machine. Sometimes I hit a jackpot like “Going Going Gone,” with its revised lyrics about “diamonds and rust,” a nod—or a shot?—at Baez. Other times I get bupkis—yet another by-the-numbers edition of “Oh Sister.”

It’s worth noting that The 1976 Live Recordings, like previous releases of the 1966, 1974, and 1975 tours, isn’t being marketed as part of the Bootleg Series. The first Bootleg volume—released all the way back in 1991, now closer to the beginning of Bob’s career than it is to the present—set a high standard for classic rock box sets. Deep, voluminous, and impeccably sequenced, the inaugural release presented an extraordinary alternate history of The Great American Artist, one nearly as strong as the actual history. Even if selections were weighted toward Dylan’s first decade, a number of brilliant recordings from Bob’s wilderness years were also included. See “Lord Protect My Child,” a powerfully vulnerable ballad from the Infidels sessions. See also the alternate take of “When The Night Comes Falling From The Sky,” featuring the hot-rod stylings of Roy Bittan and Little Steven Van Zandt. “Blind Willie McTell,” “Foot of Pride,” “Series of Dreams”—the list goes on and on. My favorite Bob record shifts with the seasons; there are simply too many colors in the man’s mind to settle on one. Sometimes, however, the answer to that question is the last disc of the first volume of the Bootleg Series. It is that good.

Whatever its merits, I won’t ever say the same about The 1976 Live Recordings. Rather than present a considered set of highlights from the ‘76 run, Bob Dylan Industries has simply thrown open the gates of the vault. The words of William Mulholland upon the opening of the Los Angeles Aqueduct come to mind: “There it is, take it.” Those of us familiar with the Expecting Rain message boards have had it for years—most of it, anyway. I had my fingers crossed that someone would have rustled up a tape of Salt Lake City (5/25/76), which featured the only-ever performance of “Lily, Rosemary, and the Jack of Hearts,” but no such luck. If a tape of that show does exist, it’s still sitting in a tomb somewhere, waiting for someone to ride through the devilish cold and find it.

That, more than anything, is the central disappointment of The 1976 Live Recordings: there’s very little here that hasn’t already been in circulation for some time. Of course, bringing new and heretofore unknown delights to light was never the primary purpose. Neither was telling a story in the manner of Open Window. A release like this will surely boost the cultural footprint of Rolling Thunder ‘76, particularly amongst lower echelons of Dylan fans—those who do most of their listening through YouTube and have no idea what a FLAC is—but that’s more a happy byproduct than a raison d’etre.

The real aim here is purely legal: the maintenance and extension of copyright. EU law dictates that recordings published within 50 years of their creation are protected for 70 years following their publication. Miss that deadline and the recording enters public domain, allowing any interested parties to do with it what they will. This simple fact explains the last decade-plus of releases from Bob’s archives: The 1966 Live Recordings in 2016, The 1974 Live Recordings in 2024, and now The 1976 Live Recordings in 2026. There’s a lot of juice left to squeeze in these lemons, and Sony Music is intent on squeezing them.

The general attitude of Bob Dylan Industries seems to be that any scrap of music ever made by Dylan is worth preserving and exercising ownership over. There is a cold, calculating logic behind these box sets, one which prioritizes financial motives over the music itself. The 1976 material would benefit greatly from the deft hand of a curator, someone who had dedicated the time to separate the wheat from the chaff (releasing the complete Fort Worth show on streaming services is a poor substitute). This careful editorial approach is what makes the inaugural Bootleg Series release or Through The Open Window such powerful collections. In this case, however, it would yield an incomplete copyright arrangement. So here we are instead.

Fine by me. Even if The 1976 Live Recordings ends up being too much of a good thing—seriously, if I ever hear another “Vincent Van Gogh,” it’ll be too soon—I can’t say I’m dissatisfied with the finished product. If anything, it makes me excited for the years to come, as later Dylan tours approach their semicentennial.

I’ve long been obsessed with the 1978 shows, for instance. That year’s incarnation of Dylan featured radically glitzy rearrangements, powerhouse Street-Legal cuts, and a plethora of ruffled shirts. The At Budokan live album documented a specimen from the early days of the tour, but the best performances came at the end, as Bob refined the schmaltzy big band sound into something soulful and desperate. I’ll be first in line for a hypothetical 50-disc The 1978 Live Recordings set. Then there’s the gospel tours of ‘79 and ‘80, and the “Bob Is Back” run from ‘81, and the butt rock and eyeliner era from ‘84… It goes on and on.

The important thing is that this music was made, and now it is being made available. Copyright holders and Dylan obsessives can agree on that much, even if we’re getting different things out of a release like The 1976 Live Recordings. We always did feel the same, we just saw it from a different point of view.

The gothic horror movie depicts mysterious events at a 19th-century English estate after a strange new governess arrives.

To celebrate the theatrical release on November 13, the film's souvenir popcorn bucket has officially arrived—and it’s a bloody Victorian baby doll.

The movie studio describes it as “the most devilishly macabre popcorn bucket of its kind.” That’s not an understatement. The doll has mottled skin, a terrifying face, and a bloody open hole in its torso to hold your popcorn.

True to the time period, the doll comes with a Victorian-era bonnet and baby clothes. The promotional photos also feature an ornate wooden cradle, with a lid that pushes it further into coffin territory.

Author and podcast host Rose Dommu got a firsthand look at the new popcorn bucket at an advance screening, and it somehow looks even freakier in real life.

Social media users, understandably, have thoughts. “The coffin/crib is cool, but the actual bucket is the dead baby part?? That’s…odd,” one X user wrote. “I get horror. But this is just vulgar and tactless,” another added.

Most commenters so far don’t seem to be huge fans of the doll, but a few appreciate how campy it is. “Yes girl let’s eat some dead baby popcorn,” one social media user joked.

This isn’t the only wacky popcorn bucket we’ve seen this year. Just last week, AMC debuted the Dune 3 souvenir bucket that contains not one, but two sandworms. Details about the Victorian Psycho popcorn bucket—including the price and where to buy it—have yet to be revealed. But it’s already clear that this might be the most unhinged popcorn bucket we’ve seen yet.

#6668. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6667. Dutch Apple Pie

Dutch apple pie is the upgrade the fall classic needs. With a nutty, streusel topping, this cozy dessert will have you coming back for slice after slice. It’s also easier to make than the traditional version because there’s no need to cook the apple filling ahead of time. In fact, some of us will be swapping out our traditional apple pie recipe for this one for Thanksgiving this year.

Lightly flour your work surface, then roll out the chilled dough into a 12-inch circle. Carefully move it to a 9-inch pie dish. Gently lift the edges and let the dough settle into the pan. Make sure not to stretch the dough. Press it firmly into the bottom and sides. Pop it in the fridge until it’s cold (about 30 minutes), or freeze it for 10 minutes if you’re in a hurry.

Grab a medium bowl and whisk together the granulated sugar, flour, cinnamon, and salt.

In a large bowl, whisk together the egg, sour cream, and vanilla. Add the dry ingredients and whisk until the mixture is nice and smooth.

Move a rack to the center of your oven and preheat it to 350°. In a medium bowl, whisk together the brown sugar, flour, granulated sugar, walnuts, oats, and cinnamon. Add the butter and use a fork or pastry cutter to work it in until crumbly.

Spread the apples evenly in your prepared pie crust. Pour the filling over the apples, then sprinkle the crumble topping all over.

Bake the pie until the crust and crumble are golden brown and you don’t see any more moisture. This should take about an hour. Once it’s done, let the pie cool on a wire rack until it reaches room temperature, then pop it in the fridge for an hour before serving.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Because this pie has a sour cream and egg-based filling, store leftovers covered in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

#6666. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6665. The Real-Life Wardrobe of Jamie Campbell Bower, Who Only Wears Suits If They’re McQueen

“I don’t know, I suppose I’m an artist,” Jamie Campbell Bower says with a laugh, after I ask him to describe himself. He’s correct, in more ways than one. If you’ve been consuming pop culture for the last decade and change, it’s less a matter of if you’ve seen the 37-year-old Londoner before, but where. He’s acted in some of the biggest franchises in Hollywood—including Twilight, Harry Potter, The Mortal Instruments, and Stranger Things—while also nurturing a multifaceted music career. As of this month, he’ll be heading to Middle-earth as Celeborn in the third season of Amazon Prime’s epic Lord of the Rings series, The Rings of Power.

During a hectic week of Rings of Power in New York City, Bower and I spent a quiet early morning talking about the bands that helped him find his style as a teenager, the difference between performing as an actor and a musician, and why he loves playing the bad guy.

All clothing and accessories, subject’s own. Coat by MM6 Maison Margiela. Sweater by John Lawrence Sullivan. Vintage skirt. Shoes by John Lawrence Sullivan. Sunglasses by Persol (throughout). Jewelry by Pianegonda.

Jamie Campbell Bower: It’s complexity. With any character, there has to be a level of complexity. Playing in the shadow self is really illuminating, to be Jungian. You have to know it in order for it to not take over. I found it particularly interesting to rationale and reason, even though this character was doing terrible things. I have always found it really interesting to dig away and find the why. So much of that character was really about isolation and pain and not feeling like they had a sense of belonging in the space for them. Obviously, they find this power that gives them this sense of safety. It becomes the wall, and it gives them purpose, and it hides them from the world and from being hurt. What draws me to any character is complexity and understanding the balance. It’s almost anthropological in a way.

It was amazing. I was so terrified on day one. I’m always nervous about joining any show, doing any gig. But I remember day one of actually shooting with other cast members, turning around to Nick Müller, our A-camera operator, and I just went, “Look, Nick, you’ve been here way longer than I have. If I’m in your way, just tell me to fucking move.”

I’d been a part of Twilight as well—joined that on the second movie after watching a cultural moment explode—and I was in that position again with Stranger Things. It was so big. I was joining this new world, but everyone was wicked and super kind. I made some amazing friends. I love Millie [Bobby Brown]. She’s just the best. She’s like my little sister, and also like my big sister at times as well. She’s got so much sage advice and is so brilliant at what she does and so driven. I am in awe of her, and I was from the moment I met her.

I’ve got the hand of Vecna. I took it out on Fallon [the other] night. I told this story, but I got my bag searched in Mexico City on the way in over the weekend. We pulled up and one of the people there looked at me—her eyes got big. She said, “Vecna.” I’ve got three massive fuck-off suitcases. They’re going through them and I’m like, “Look, I’ve got the hand of Vecna in here. Do you want to see it?” And then it ended up being the quickest bag search ever. I got some elf ears with me as well, both made by the same guy, Barrie Gower.

It was the summer when I was 15. I spent it wearing a visor with spiky hair, because I used to skate growing up in super baggy jeans. I remember turning up being like, “That’s not you.” Skating is a part of who I am, but I was looking to represent myself in some way, shape, or form.

Then we started this indie band when I was 16, 17. Devonté Hynes had this band called Test Icicles. I always used to look at those guys with their skinny jeans and their big hair, and I was just like, “That’s a bit of me, that.” How skinny can my jeans get? How drain pipe-y am I? That’s where I really started to find my own identity.

I’ve been fortunate enough throughout my career to meet and work with such beautiful creative people in fashion and find myself more within that, too. I was talking about it to somebody yesterday: When you try a fit on that is not you, it’s like having a bad haircut. You don’t want to do that. I’m even the same if I’m doing a photoshoot. I always go through the rail and I’ll say, “That’s not my vibe. I can’t say that I’m going to wear that.” Of course, I’m always willing to try, I’m always willing to push. But you know yourself better as you get older.

It was from Alexander McQueen. I loved the identity of that brand, but I couldn’t afford a jacket, or a suit, or even a scarf. But the smaller pieces, the rings and the wallets, were like 100 bucks. Those were the things that I would gravitate towards and buy.

More recently, within the last 10 years, I remember coming here to New York for a show that I did called Will, going to Bergdorf, and buying a couple of pairs of Comme des Garçons trousers. As they were being rung up, I was like, “All right.” It wasn’t loads—we’re not talking thousands—but it was still a lot of money. That was probably the first big clothing purchase that I ever made. And I’ve still got the trousers. I used to wear them on stage in the band as well, which is foolish.

Got a bunch of stuff from H. Lorenzo the other day—some great shirts, some great jackets. I really like how they curate the store. My most recent purchase is a lot of stuff from the new Ann Demeulemeester collection. I actually just bought a sick leather trench from it—brown leather, which is fire.

Jacket by Thom Browne. Shirt, jeans, shoes by Ann Demeulemeester.

Going back to when we were kids: Test Icicles, the Libertines, the Rakes, Franz Ferdinand, Editors. Got to meet a few of those guys throughout my travels, which was always pretty sick. Nick Cave. Warren Ellis. Nick has got such a sharp style, as does Warren. Warren’s a bit more unbuttoned. I met Warren in Venice five years ago. He was stood at the end of the pier and I was so excited to meet him, I just bounded up. I was like, “Hi, Mr. Ellis. My name’s Jamie.” And I just blurted out to him for ages, and then I was like, “Thank you so much.” He said, "Good to meet you, mate. Bye.”

I think fluidity and being myself is always the main thing. I’ve never felt wholly comfortable in a regular suit. I remember we were invited to do a show in Venice, and the band that we were in was pretty heavy. We wore suits in an environment that for us felt almost quite subversive. The music that we played didn’t really fit that. I quite enjoyed that.

But on the whole, I don’t love suits too much. I like to keep it more interesting and fluid. I’m not saying that they can’t be interesting for other people, but I’ve never been interested [in them myself]. Apart from McQueen, but that’s because something like the McQueen shoulder is so identifiable and creates such an incredible silhouette. That’s probably the only time I’ve ever really been like, “I can wear this suit for a long time.” But yeah, I avoid anything that doesn’t feel right for me.

It’s hard to say. I do feel like so often they can blend. I’ve been so fortunate in my career, being drawn to things that feel like me and getting to explore different parts of myself on film. That does have an effect on the music that I’m making at the time.

With a film or a television series, you’re saying someone else’s words and building a character, but also at times injecting your own personal experience into that. In music, they are your words. You can make a choice to be like, “I’m going to build a world in this song to express something.” Or I can just be like, “This is me.” So, they can scratch different itches, but I think that they work in symbiosis sometimes.

The original movies came out when I was 12, so they were pretty seminal. I remember being in Hong Kong on a trip when The Hobbit was coming out. I was on my own, and I went to a cinema in a place called Pacific Place to watch it. That made a really big impact on me—it felt like a fantastical world that I could see myself in.

I started auditioning for it in 2024. Walking into it, of course, I was elated. I felt so lucky and so happy, like I was a little kid again. Like, I was 11 or 12 on stage in some provincial town outside of London, and now I get to fuckin’ walk into this Lord of the Rings world and be an elf? Dude, that’s sick.

Three non-negotiable albums that everyone… Oh, bloody Nora!

I discovered Dylan when I was like 16, when we were reading [J. D.] Salinger and Allen Ginsberg and books like On the Road. Let’s go with a classic. Freewheelin’ is old-school enough. It’s cool, pre-him going electric, which I adore as well. Highway 61 Revisited is a great record too. Take your pick between those two. Chopin’s Nocturnes are amazing. That’s a beautiful, beautiful piece to get into. Then there’s Nick Cave. I did an interview before and I chose Murder Ballads, which is a great record. But I also love some of the more recent work, like Ghosteen or Skeleton Tree. Ghosteen is amazing.

Oh, Ghosteen’s wicked. Let’s go with that. I referenced the artwork for Ghosteen on my last release. My album cover was by an artist called Thomas Cole, who did a collection of paintings about the journey from birth to death. He also did paintings of the Garden of Eden. From what I have now seen, those paintings heavily inspired the artist that did the paintings for Ghosteen as well, which is kind of insane.

So, he’s from the East. It’s the swearing.

#6661. A Look Inside WELL/BEINGS’s ‘Bound by Nature’ Gala

On November 6, cultural leaders, philanthropists, and conservation advocates braved the rain in New York City for a worthy cause. That evening, WELL/BEINGS hosted its annual benefit dinner at Hearst Tower, bringing guests together to support conservation efforts in the most vital and vulnerable ecosystems across the Caribbean and the Bolivian Amazon.

The event, titled “Bound by Nature” this year, was hosted by actor, entrepreneur, and philanthropist Oliver Trevena, and presented by the nonprofit’s co-founders Amanda Hearst Rønning and Breanna Schultz. Throughout the night, attendees enjoyed live music, conservation storytelling, an exclusive auction of fine art, jewelry, and luxury experiences, as well as a specially curated culinary experience by celebrity chef Eduardo Garcia.

As nods to the marine and terrestrial environments, the sea of guests wore shades of blue and green, respectively.

The benefit sought to raise funds toward more than $800,000 in programmatic commitments WELL/BEINGS has made to 15 conservation partners for 2026 and 2027. The selected organizations, which include local and underserved groups, are working to protect wildlife, restore critical habitats, and strengthen communities in targeted areas.

During her opening remarks, Hearst Rønning underscored the importance of investing in the people closest to the ecosystems in need of protection: “That is why we support and amplify local leaders,” she said. “They know what needs to be done. Too often, what stands between them and doing it is support and funding.”

Schultz echoed that sentiment, reminding attendees of the lasting impact of their contributions: “Our partners fight every day to protect what we love. Tonight, we can give them the resources to keep going…what we save now is what the next generation will inherit.”

Since its founding, WELL/BEINGS has invested more than $3 million in conservation. The organization also operates under a 100 percent donation model, with its co-founders and Board of Directors separately covering core operating expenses so that public donations go directly toward the mission at hand.

The evening also marked the launch of the Caribbean Bioregional Hub, a new initiative connecting nine partner organizations across the region to strengthen collaboration and advance coordinated conservation efforts. The sky is the limit!

Ecleen Luzmila Caraballo is the weekend editor at ELLE who covers celebrity and culture news. She was previously a senior editor at Complex and has contributed to other publications including GQ and Nylon. Born and raised in New York City to Panamanian parents, she’ll take book recs in English, Spanish (and soon, German). Her interests include music, fashion, beauty, film, earth science, and the study of love. On her time off, you can find her with loved ones at an odd-hour movie showtime, baking, or sitting in silence near a high-fidelity sound system.

#6660. 11 Best Cowboy Boots in 2026, According to GQ Editors

You might think that cowboy boots are a privilege reserved for ranch hands and folks who can actually ride a horse. But with a little chutzpah, the best cowboy boots are just as adept on a saddle as they are on the subway. Is that so surprising? Before they blossomed into their fashionable forms, much of menswear’s most riffed on garments were rooted in function: cargo pants, work jackets, even suits. With enough time, they were adopted by civilians and adapted to their second lives as symbols of self-expression and creativity, not just job uniforms. Cowboy boots are no different.

In terms of styling, the classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with some well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage boot cuts) and with a snap shirt. And that's still a great approach. But if you open up your mind and step outside of the saloon, the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a ‘70s-inspired suit screams filthy rich oil tycoon if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or, why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots. So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

And if you’re having trouble, well, that’s why you’re here. We’ve wrangled together the best cowboy boots west—and east—of the Mississippi, from the budget-friendly to the ostentatious and every vibe in-between.

The good folks at Tecovas are living, breathing proof that direct-to-consumer brands aren’t all operated by algorithms tasked with solving imaginary problems. The DTC upstart might be the youngest of the bootmakers on this list, but it's quickly endeared itself to budget-strapped swashbucklers with a hankering for democratically-priced kicks.

Take, for example, the Cartwright, a handsome riff on a classic western silhouette made in Leon, Mexico, a bona fide cobbling capital of the world with over a century of expertise to draw on. It boasts hand-laid cording at the shaft, a resoleable Goodyear-welt construction, and a slew of colors and leathers to choose from, including genuine cowhide and goat leather. They’re not the cheapest boots on this list, but the relatively approachable price belies the craftsmanship involved. For $375, they’re one small step up from our favorite budget cowboy boots—but one giant leap in overall quality.

You can think of roper boots as the chilled-out version of the average western boot. Originally designed for calf roping, roper boots feature a shorter shaft and a shorter, squared off heel. These details made it easier for cowboys to dismount their horse and run after the calves they roped. Coincidentally, they also make roper boots easier to walk in which is why some people prefer them over other cowboy boots for everyday wear.

Our pick for the best roper boots currently goes to Red Wing. (Perhaps no surprise, given the brand also makes our favorite trend-proof boots.) Part of Red Wing's Heritage line, they're crafted with premium S.B. Foot Tanning Company leather, and feature Goodyear welt construction so you can have them resoled and keep ‘em going for a long time. Plus, if you’re just dipping your toes into the cowboy boot world, the minimalist uppers forgo the decorative western stitching which makes them easier to style.

If you’re after that western look but need a pair of boots that can handle the demands of a jobsite, a lot of guys will tell you to look to Ariat. That’s because they manage to blend classic cowboy style with modern-day features, and a palatable price point in perfect proportion. While they do offer a range of work boots in lace-up styles, their Groundbreaker boots are a standout with classic cowboy boot looks.

They’re made of full-grain leather, include a supportive and comfortable insole, and meet ASTM standards for slip resistance and electrical safety. Because it’s among Ariat’s most popular styles, it’s also available in a wide range of colorways, toe shapes, and even steel toe versions. Some more traditional cowboys will poo-poo the fact that these aren’t made stateside, but if you’re on a budget, you’ll get more than what you pay for.

Cowboy boots aren’t all rough-and-tumble affairs. In fact, the right pair can easily strut the red carpet or waltz into a fancy restaurant with panache. You’ll want a pair with leather that shines up well and in a darker colorway. For date nights and more formal affairs, these Tony Lamas will impress thanks to the exotic lizard skin uppers and low-key embroidery. They’re the kind of boots that can play well for the in-laws with a tailored suit or play a rock-’n’-roll star with some vintage jeans and a tight white tee.

These days, most boot brands walk in the shadows of one brand: Lucchese. They’ve been outfitting American presidents, high-profile celebs, and the Dallas Cowboy Cheerleaders for decades and it’s all thanks to their commitment to high-quality craftsmanship. Though any pair of Lucchese’s would earn you more than a few approving head nods, the most coveted are the boots that they make in their Texas workshop.

Using a range of full-grain leathers and exotic leathers like caiman alligator and pirarucu fish skin, each pair is crafted by master bootmakers using time-honored techniques. The Gavin, in their iconic Black Cherry, is a picture-perfect style featuring smooth Santini goat leather uppers with intricate embellishments, welted construction, and lemonwood pegs—made the old-fashioned way, basically. They’ll cost you a pretty penny, of course, but they'll last pretty much forever, and the drip you’ll get in return is priceless.

From Ralph Lauren’s western-inspired sub-label, these RRL boots meld high-end materials with old-world craftsmanship and feature American-tanned leather uppers, Goodyear-welted construction, and vintage-style rubber soles—all crafted in a multi-generational Texas bootmaking factory.

Frye is another American brand with proven boot quality chops. (In fact, it claims to be America's oldest continually-operating boot company.) Its Roper boot has all the same strengths as Red Wing's, and comes in a non-roughout leather.

We don't typically include the same designers twice on one list, but Tecovas are that good. The Johnny is for anyone who wants a softer, slightly more charming boot than the eternal Cartwright up top.

For fellas whose style skews a little more regular-guy than rodeo, these lower-profile, lower-priced Ropers have a Goodyear welt and Vibram outsole. Bang for your, ahem, buck.

Wythe's playing-card-inspired boots feature all the bells and whistles, including premium leather inside and out, hand-applied details, lemonwood pegs, and second-to-none construction all-around. While some brands tap the expert bootmakers in Léon, Mexico to pump out high-quality mass-appeal boots, Wythe tapped these artisans to really let them cook.

All of Yuketen's shoes are perfect, which is a big part of the reason Drake's now carries them. And while they're best known for their moccasin styles, the brand makes an exceptionally handsome cowboy boot too. Really, they're just showing off now.

The classic move for western boots is to lean into their rougher side. Toss them on with well-fitting jeans (preferably vintage bootcuts) and a snap-button shirt. But open up your mind and step outside of the saloon and the possibilities are practically endless. A slick pair of exotic leather cowboy boots matched with a '70s-inspired suit screams filthy-rich oil tycoon—if not Alessandro Michele-era Gucci. Or why not mix up a preppy pair of chinos with a grungy graphic tee and some roughed-up suede ropers? The point is, you don’t have to pretend to be a cowboy to wear their boots (though you certainly can). So treat them like any other pair of shoes in your closet and wear them however you want. Hell, we’d go so far as to call them an essential pair of boots for every wardrobe.

Peter Middleton knows a thing or two about the lifestyle having cut his teeth at Ralph Lauren and used it as a springboard for his own western-inspired brand, Wythe. “To me the beauty and shape of the Cowboy Boot (and a lot of the original design intent) lies in its curves and that’s what makes a great boot SEXY. There isn't a lot of men's footwear that has these dramatic curves, leather, and a high heel but the right cowboy boot has them all.”

He says that good cowboy boots should be made with natural leathers that age well with wear, mould to the wearer’s feet, and can be recrafted repeatedly. His non-negotiables include full leather construction from the insole to the outsole, linings, uppers, and heels. Look for Goodyear welted construction which will allow you to have the boots resoled and extend their life. The toe bug (the fancy stitching at the toe), should sit right where your foot flexes to help cover up the crease that comes with each step. Preferably, this would be corded by hand, of course.

Price points will vary, and you can get some well-made boots for around $300. The really great stuff will often be twice that much. Middleton says, “the best thing to do is wait and save up until you can buy the version you actually want because its impossible to cut corners and still deliver the product you want.” So if you can be patient, save up. If you can’t, try buying secondhand. But if you simply can’t wait, you’ll do well enough with plenty of the mid-tier brands until you’re ready to upgrade.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you.

#6659. We Tried The World-Famous Apple Pie In A Bag—Is It Worth The Hype?

Delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Thanksgiving is only a few weeks away, so it’s already time to start planning your holiday menu. And with so many labor-intensive savory dishes on my list, I prefer to outsource dessert to the pros. Grocery store pies are often average at best, but there’s one out there that might actually be better than homemade.

The Elegant Farmer is a family-owned business based in Mukwonago, Wisconsin. In addition to operating an orchard with a dozen apple varieties, they’re best known as a specialty food store—largely thanks to its award-winning Apple Pie in a Paper Bag.

Over the past several decades, the signature dessert has achieved national acclaim and developed a cult following. Gourmet and The Wall Street Journal have dubbed it the best apple pie in America, and The Elegant Farmer even bested Bobby Flay in a 2008 episode of Throwdown.

Now, dessert lovers nationwide can get one of these famous pies delivered through Goldbelly. However, a single pie costs a whopping $70, including shipping. But is the Apple Pie in a Paper Bag worth the hype—and the sticker shock? I got my hands on one to find out.

The bag isn’t just a marketing schtick. 26 years ago, The Elegant Farmer’s former owners, Dan and Karen Scheel, wanted to sell a new dessert using the apples grown in their orchard. Karen found a recipe in a cookbook for a pie baked in a paper bag, so she enlisted their team of bakers to develop their own version.

The paper bag offers two benefits. The sealed environment traps moisture as it bakes to keep the Ida Red apples juicy, but it also prevents the crust from burning. Partway through baking, The Elegant Farmer cuts a hole in the center of the bag so that the top crust is perfectly golden by the end.

When you order this pie, it arrives pre-baked and frozen in a shrink-wrapped cardboard box. All you need to do is warm it straight from frozen in a 325°F oven for about an hour. If you thaw it in the refrigerator first, you can reheat it at 425°F for just 8 to 10 minutes. Yes, it’s that easy.

The instructions direct you to place the pie on a baking tray, but I’d recommend going one step further and laying down a protective layer of parchment first. A considerable amount of caramelized sugar collects at the bottom of the bag and can leak into the oven. Adding the extra barrier is a simple step that spares you from scrubbing it off later.

An hour later, the pie was warm and ready to serve. The torn paper and cracked crust admittedly don’t make this the most visually stunning pie in the world. But once our editors took a bite, any aesthetic concerns went out the window.

Contributing Writer Steven Morea said the apples taste like “they were just picked.” Digital Director Katelyn Lunders appreciated the abundance of apples and how the filling wasn’t too sweet. “I can’t stop eating it,” she added. (Lunders is already planning on ordering another for her family Thanksgiving, by the way.)

The crust got equally rave reviews. “I would buy this just for the crust,” said Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy. The pronounced butter flavor, golden caramelization, and crunchy texture perfectly offset the softness of the fruit. Even Digital Community Editor Taylor Worden—a self-proclaimed pie hater—fell in love with it. And Test Kitchen Manager Alejandro Valdes Lora kept his opinion short and sweet: “I’m obsessed with this.”

If our office’s unanimous praise is any indication, The Elegant Farmer’s Apple Pie in a Paper Bag is absolutely worth the hype. We may hesitate to spend $70 on this pie on any ordinary day. But for special occasions like Thanksgiving, it’s a convenient showstopper that’ll easily upstage everything else on your holiday menu.

#6658. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6656. Dakota Johnson Dons Diamonds and a Hoodie for Date Night With Machine Gun Kelly

Dakota Johnson has always had a certain rock-and-roll sensibility to her style, be it the perfectly undone hair, the flash of skin amid the lace and monochromatic, a suite of very good denim. But lately, as her rumored romance with Machine Gun Kelly seems to be gathering momentum, the actor looks to be leaning a little further into her rock-star era. And what better way to do so than with a hoodie and six figures worth of diamonds?

On Thursday evening, Johnson attended a Khaite-hosted dinner at Dan Tana’s in West Hollywood, where she was also spotted with Kelly. For the occasion, she mixed the decidedly high and low: a black zip-up hoodie emblazoned with the red logo of Death Row Pictures, Snoop Dogg’s production company, worn over a black Valentino crepe miniskirt with delicate lace trimming. She added a pair of knee-high black Gucci Horsebit boots and a quilted Valentino Rockstud Spike shoulder bag.

Johnson then layered a tiger’s-eye and diamond necklace by Laoli, complete with a diamond clasp pendant, with Jessica McCormack’s Signature 42-carat Diamond Button Back Necklace. (McCormack being the cool-girl jeweler also beloved by Zoe Kravitz.) It brought serious sparkle to an otherwise off-duty ensemble.

Machine Gun Kelly, meanwhile, wore an emerald-green satin bomber jacket over a bright yellow hoodie, with loose gray sweatpants, a black beanie, and a red bandana pulled across his face. The pair, who reportedly left the restaurant separately, might have very different approaches to getting dressed, but there’s an increasingly complementary spirit in their shared taste for casual, slightly rebellious pieces.

As for Dakota Johnson’s enviable wardrobe, she’s hardly a stranger to the more provocative side of fashion. Valentino, in particular, has long provided her with a means of balancing romantic femininity with something a little darker and more subversive. And while her love of lace, abbreviated hemlines, and slouchy outerwear predates Kelly, the musician’s punkish influence is there.

#6654. Crock-Pot Chicken Noodle Soup

The pinnacle of cozy, comforting food is chicken noodle soup. When you need something warming and satisfying, there’s just nothing better. While our classic recipe is already easy to whip up, tossing all of your ingredients in the slow cooker makes this soup easier than ever. After a few hours and very little effort, you’ll have the coziest meal on your hands, ready to warm you up all fall and winter long.

What People Are Saying:“Perfect for snow days. Easy to make and there is no wrong time for soup” - evabnyc2372

“ Very easy....very good thank god I made a big pot bc I have 3 boys my oldest had 5 servings and my youngest had two giant servings my middle son had 3” - ashleybaby3586

The best thing about this recipe? It’s not necessary to cook the chicken before putting it in the soup—let your slow cooker do all the hard work for you. Place the boneless, skinless chicken breasts in the slow cooker, along with the veggies, herbs, butter, and broth. Season with salt and pepper, then cook on high with the lid closed for 2 1/2 hours.

By now, the chicken should be cooked and tender. Transfer it to a plate, and after letting it cool slightly, use 2 forks to shred it (or whatever is your favorite shredding method).

Discard the thyme, rosemary, and bay leaf from the slow cooker, then add the shredded chicken back in along with the egg noodles. Cover and cook on High for about 5 to 10 minutes—you're looking for the noodles to be al dente.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have leftovers, I strongly suggest that you store the noodles separately from the broth. If they’re stored together, the noodles will soak up the liquid and turn to mush, and there won’t be any broth left. If you’d like to cook this soup in advance, the same recommendation applies, though if you’re making it ahead of time, I'd recommend skipping the noodles completely. You can add them to the broth when you reheat the soup, and they should be fully cooked in just 5 minutes.

Same deal if you're freezing—the soup itself freezes well and can be reheated whenever the craving hits, but the noodles will get mushy sitting in all of that broth, so I'd recommend cooking them off fresh!

#6653. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6651. Dry Brushing: Why I Do It Every Day And All The Benefits

It seems like every time I watch a get-ready-with-me video, the first step of the routine is dry brushing. And while I’ve tried it here and there, I never found myself committing to the act. But this skin-care practice is beloved by not only the likes of Gwyneth Paltrow and Tracee Ellis Ross, but also by functional health doctors and medical professionals as well.

So what is dry brushing? It’s the act of running a bristled brush across your skin while working against gravity (so working toward your torso on limbs) to help with moving the body’s lymphatic system.

Everybody raves about the myriad of health benefits that comes along with dry brushing—from physically exfoliating your skin and eliminating strawberry skin to increasing blood flow and potentially diminishing the appearance of circulation.

Perhaps, then, it’s time to really give it a try.

True to its name, dry brushing involves running a bristled brush over dry skin, most commonly on the body (though occasionally, on the face if you’re working with a face-specific brush that’s much softer). “It is a powerful Ayurvedic practice that both exfoliates the skin and opens detox pathways to support lymphatic drainage and boost immunity,” says Lauren Berlingeri, co-founder of HigherDose.

A simple pre-shower ritual, it isn’t just used in Ayurvedic medicine to stimulate the skin and the body’s lymphatic system, but in traditional Chinese medicine (a.k.a. TCM) too. It’s a practice that has stood the test of time, which is always a good sign when trying to understand whether a wellness “trend” is really worth its salt.

As well as stimulating lymphatic drainage, which helps in detoxifying the body, dry brushing is supposed to be effective for removing dead skin cells to smooth skin, boosting blood circulation, and reducing puffiness and water retention. It is a great way to invigorate body and mind, especially at the start of the day. And some say it’s also great at reducing the appearance of cellulite, but from my personal research, this seems somewhat unfounded.

Sophie Bolvary, licensed massage therapist at Sanara, adds that the practice of dry brushing may boost our immune system: “The lymphatic system does not have a ‘pump’ of its own, meaning it only gets working when we start moving our body or when it is stimulated manually by dry brushing or light massage,” she explains.

She adds that different brushes can have a different effect on the body. Dry brushes made with boar-hair bristles are ideal for daily use and exfoliation. Dry brushes with ionic-copper bristles carry the added benefit of sweeping your body in negative ions, which is known for antiviral and antibacterial properties in traditional medicine. It also may bring us full body-mind refreshment as an added self-care benefit.

“The brisk rhythmic motion creates a sensory reset that I find both grounding and energizing,” Bolvary adds. “Helping to sharpen mental alertness and brighten my mood.” Pro tip: Sprinkle an essential-oil blend (like something with citrus) to your dry brush to further wake up your senses.

I’ve used a dry body brush during episodic health kicks previously, but rarely consistently—but my coworker swears by it before every shower, especially when she’s taking an “Everything Shower.” What I’ve most noticed since making it (at least) a four-times-a-week thing is that my skin is infinitely looking more polished and brighter. It’s an excellent way to quickly slough off the dead skin cells that form a grey veil over what was months before a summer tan, and it’s certainly a good way to wake yourself up in the morning.

I have found that combining it with a “contrast” shower—i.e., turning the temperature hot, then cold, then hot, then cold—makes me feel extremely energized, particularly after a vigorous workout. You also don’t really need to commit to doing five minutes to reap the benefits—give it three minutes and you’ll feel fantastic as you start your day. It’s worth noting that—as hard as I willed it—dry brushing won’t stimulate lymphatic drainage enough to cure a hangover. This is deeply disappointing, but I continue to search for a fix.

Newbies to the practice should know that once you’ve dry-brushed, you’ll likely experience an itchy, tingling sensation, along with some possible redness, which soon settles. This feeling quickly becomes less prominent with regular use, but it’s actually a sign that your circulation is revved up and blood is en route to the surface of the skin.

You also might feel, for lack of a better way to phrase it, like your skin is dusty. This is all the dead skin cells you just exfoliated off—which is why most people prefer to do this practice before hopping in the shower. Don’t fret, a little big of your favorite body soap will take care of it.

Dry body brushing is a really easy—and affordable—ritual to commit to, which is why it gets a yes from me. You can’t always see the many benefits it has on the body, but you can often feel them. I have personally noticed a more even skin tone, slightly lighter-feeling legs (not yet as streamlined as Paltrow’s, unfortunately), and more morning vitality. I also firmly believe that taking a few intentional minutes to do something positive for your well-being each day is underrated.

Next up… time to crack body moisturizing. A look at the dry brushes we’d recommend, below.

There are a few negative side effects that can occur if you’re not careful. Marisa Garshick, MD, board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology, says that it may cause irritation or micro-tears in the skin if too much pressure is applied. You’ll also want to consider what skin conditions you might be dealing with and if your skin type can tolerate all this brushing. Dr. Garshick says it’s not recommended for anyone with sensitive, broken, or inflamed skin like eczema or psoriasis.

Bolvary adds that you’ll want to be mindful about cleaning your brush (more on how to do that later). Because of the exfoliating nature of dry brushing, there could be a lot of skin-shedding debris that builds up in the brush that can make dry brushing ineffective or irritate your skin further.

Dr. Garshick says that dry brushing can be done one to two times a week if you have sensitive skin, as frequent brushing might cause irritation. But if your skin can tolerate it, Bolvary says that it can be a daily practice. She recommends doing it at the start of your day, right before hopping in the shower. “Some people find it more stimulating and energizing than a cup of coffee,” she says. Here’s to hoping.

Dry brushing done by a professional will give you a more in-depth treatment. “The practitioner takes care of the work, and reaches all the hard-to-reach areas, while you simply enjoy the awakening sensations,” says Bolvary. “Also, the practitioner can demonstrate proper technique and pressure for your skin and body type.”

But that doesn’t mean doing it at home won’t have its own benefits. She says it’s helpful to look at a lymphatic glow map: “A very easy Google search, which can outline the general flow of lymph and how to sweep into the main lymph ports of the body.” After a few tries on your own, she says, you get used to it.

Bolvary says that because dry brushes are usually made with natural materials, it’s best to use natural, non-chemical cleaning solutions to clean your brushes. “I like to get a bowl of warm water with several drops of tea tree oil and place the brush bristles down to let it soak for about 30 minutes. Then set it aside to dry.”

But keep in mind that your brush will soften over time and will eventually shed a little with regular washing. “These tools are not meant to last forever,” she says. “So if your brush has become too soft and the bristles are falling out with every use, it may be time for a new one.”

Try to wash your brush once every two weeks and spritz it with something like tea tree mist after every use. Bolvary also recommends leaving it in a window to air-dry rather than on your shower ledge, where it can easily get dirty.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to dry brushes, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: bristle type, texture, handle length, size, and the skin and wellness concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.
